text: The NbMoWTaRe alloy produced by high‑energy mechanical alloying and subsequent hot‑press consolidation exhibits a remarkably robust body‑centered‑cubic (BCC) matrix that persists across the examined temperature window. Rapid powder mixing promotes near‑equiatomic distribution of Nb, Mo, W, Ta, and Re, generating extensive lattice distortion that suppresses the nucleation of ordered intermetallics and stabilizes a single‑phase BCC solid solution. Hot pressing at elevated pressure further eliminates residual porosity and enhances diffusion, allowing the constituent refractory elements to occupy random lattice sites while maintaining compositional homogeneity. Electron diffraction and X‑ray patterns reveal only weak superlattice reflections, confirming the absence of secondary phases such as σ or Laves structures. Thermodynamic assessments indicate that the high configurational entropy, combined with the comparable atomic radii of the five elements, lowers the free energy of the disordered BCC configuration, thereby extending its stability to temperatures where conventional refractory alloys would typically decompose.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions

text: Both TaMoZrCrNb and TiCrTaWRe emerge from arc‑melting and rapid solidification, yet their elemental make‑up steers the balance between strength and ductility in opposite directions. The former alloy concentrates on very high melting‑point, body‑centered cubic refractory elements that generate a severe lattice‑distortion field; this solid‑solution strengthening is amplified by the presence of relatively large atomic‑size mismatches among Ta, Mo, Zr, Cr and Nb, which suppress dislocation motion and raise yield strength, but also promote early strain localization and limited work‑hardening, reducing uniform elongation. In contrast, TiCrTaWRe incorporates lighter, more ductile Ti and the more slip‑friendly HCP‑prone Cr together with the strong refractory pair Ta–W–Re; the reduced overall size mismatch and the occasional formation of nanoscale B2‑type precipitates provide moderate strengthening while preserving multiple slip systems that accommodate plastic flow, thus yielding a higher ductility at the expense of peak strength. Consequently, one would expect TaMoZrCrNb to trend toward the stronger‑but‑less‑ductile end of the spectrum, whereas TiCrTaWRe should exhibit a comparatively softer response with noticeably greater elongation before fracture.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy WTiZrReTaHf, produced by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot‑pressing, exhibits a microstructure dominated by a BCC solid‑solution matrix that retains a high degree of lattice distortion and a modest fraction of nanoscale Re‑rich precipitates along grain boundaries. Instrumented indentation studies reveal a relatively high hardness coupled with a modestly reduced elastic modulus, reflecting the combined effect of solid‑solution strengthening and the constrained deformation of the hard precipitates. Under cyclic loading, fatigue cracks preferentially nucleate at sites where the distorted lattice interacts with residual porosity or clustered Re precipitates, because these locations concentrate plastic strain and generate stress raisers. Once initiated, the cracks propagate along paths of least resistance, often threading through high‑angle grain boundaries that have been weakened by precipitate coarsening during the hot‑press cycle. The pronounced lattice strain energy and the limited strain‑hardening capacity of the BCC matrix slow crack growth, extending fatigue life, whereas a finer grain size and a more uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates tend to raise the threshold stress intensity for crack initiation and promote a more tortuous propagation path.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life

text: Mechanical alloying of the refractory high‑entropy alloys ReVTiWNb and CrWTiHfReMo followed by hot pressing generates a predominantly body‑centered cubic microstructure with fine equiaxed grains and minimal porosity. In ReVTiWNb, the high lattice distortion from the five‑element mixture, together with a relatively low tendency to form intermetallic secondary phases, promotes a more uniform grain refinement and a more homogeneous distribution of dislocations. These features suppress the nucleation of fatigue cracks and tend to increase the crack‑propagation resistance by providing a greater number of barriers to crack growth. In contrast, CrWTiHfReMo contains larger intermetallic precipitates, such as TiCr and HfMo carbides, which can act as stress concentrators. Although these precipitates contribute to solid‑solution strengthening at low temperatures, they also facilitate the initiation of fatigue cracks and accelerate crack growth due to localized strain localization. Consequently, ReVTiWNb would plausibly exhibit a longer fatigue life than CrWTiHfReMo under comparable cyclic loading conditions, mainly because of its finer grain size, lower secondary‑phase content, and reduced porosity, all of which collectively impede crack initiation and propagation.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy CrZrVReWTi, fabricated by vacuum‑induction melting and subsequent homogenization, exhibits a markedly different high‑temperature response than conventional Ni‑based superalloys. Its multicomponent matrix generates extreme lattice distortion, which together with the high melting points of Cr, Zr, V, Re, W and Ti, yields an elevated solid‑solution strengthening that sustains flow resistance well above 1000 °C where Ni‑based γ′‑strengthened alloys begin to soften. The absence of ordered γ′ precipitates eliminates the coarsening pathways typical of superalloys, while the formation of a fine dispersion of refractory‑rich BCC sub‑grains, stabilized by sluggish diffusion, impedes dislocation motion and contributes to a retained creep strength. Moreover, the inherent oxidation resistance of Cr and Ti surface oxides provides a protective scale that is less prone to spallation than the Al₂O₃‑rich layers on Ni alloys. Grain‑size refinement achieved through rapid solidification further enhances hardness and yield strength, reinforcing the alloy’s suitability for prolonged service in extreme thermal environments.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: In the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReTiV, the equiatomic mixture of rhenium, titanium, and vanadium is consolidated by vacuum induction melting, producing a homogeneous γ‑phase body‑centered cubic matrix with minimal porosity and a fine equiaxed grain structure. This contrasts with conventional Ni‑based superalloys, where γ and γ′ phases form a lattice‑distorted, lamellar microstructure that is deliberately engineered for creep resistance. ReTiV’s large atomic size mismatch and high mixing enthalpy create pronounced lattice distortion, which in turn enhances solid‑solution strengthening and suppresses dislocation motion at elevated temperatures. Because the alloy lacks a second‑phase γ′ precipitate, the high‑temperature creep behavior is governed primarily by grain‑boundary sliding and diffusional creep in the solid solution, yet the reduced grain size and strong solid‑solution effects confer a superior resistance to grain growth compared to Ni‑based counterparts. Consequently, ReTiV maintains a more stable microstructure and retains higher yield strength and hardness at temperatures where Ni‑based alloys begin to experience significant γ′ coarsening and softening, making it a promising candidate for ultra‑high‑temperature structural applications.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: The NbTaCrTiHfReV alloy, consolidated after high‑energy mechanical alloying and hot‑press densification, exhibits pronounced lattice distortion owing to the wide span of atomic radii among its constituent elements, from the relatively small Cr and V atoms to the larger Hf and Re species. This size mismatch generates a heterogeneous strain field that hampers dislocation glide, thereby raising the overall resistance to plastic deformation. The severe distortion also promotes a high degree of configurational entropy, stabilizing a single‑phase body‑centered cubic matrix while suppressing the nucleation of deleterious secondary phases during hot pressing. Residual micro‑stresses inherited from the milling process are partially relaxed during sintering, yet enough lattice curvature remains to maintain a robust solid‑solution strengthening contribution. Consequently, the alloy displays a notable increase in hardness and yield strength relative to less‑distorted refractory systems, while retaining sufficient ductility to avoid catastrophic brittle fracture.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: lattice distortion effects from atomic size mismatch

text: The TaNbTiReCrWMo alloy was fabricated by blending elemental powders (≤ 30 µm) in a planetary mill under argon, followed by consolidation in a spark‑plasma‑sintering (SPS) furnace at a peak temperature just below the solidus and a dwell time short enough to limit grain growth. Optical microscopy revealed a cellular‑like network of dendritic arms that retained the original compositional gradient imposed during milling; energy‑dispersive spectroscopy showed enrichment of the high‑density elements Re and W within the primary dendrite cores, while Nb, Ti, and Cr preferentially partitioned to the interdendritic channels. Electron backscatter diffraction maps indicated a bimodal grain structure: fine equiaxed grains (< 10 µm) bordering the interdendritic regions and coarser columnar grains (> 30 µm) extending along the dendrite trunks. The contrast between these two populations is accentuated after SPS, where the rapid heating and applied pressure suppresses extensive coarsening yet preserves the segregation pattern, providing a heterogeneous microstructure that can be tuned by adjusting the sintering pressure and cooling rate.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: microstructural features such as dendritic segregation and grain size

text: The vacuum‑induction‑melted HfZrTaCrNbTi alloy exhibits a markedly higher yield strength than the MoHfZrVTaNbRe system, a consequence of the pronounced solid‑solution strengthening generated by its larger atomic‑size mismatch and greater configurational entropy among the five transition‑metal constituents. In HfZrTaCrNbTi, the coexistence of relatively low‑density Hf and Zr with the smaller, more refractory Cr and Ti creates extensive lattice distortion, which impedes dislocation motion more effectively than the more uniformly sized Mo‑based matrix of the MoHfZrVTaNbRe alloy. Moreover, the presence of Cr and Ti promotes short‑range ordering that further raises the critical resolved shear stress, while the Mo‑rich composition experiences comparatively milder distortion and benefits from a modest amount of body‑centered‑cubic solid solution that is easier for dislocations to bypass. Consequently, the HfZrTaCrNbTi alloy is expected to trend toward superior yield strength, whereas the MoHfZrVTaNbRe alloy should display a lower, though still respectable, yield response under comparable loading conditions.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: qualitative yield strength trends and their relation to solid solution strengthening

text: The TaVZrWHf refractory high‑entropy alloy was synthesized by blending elemental powders (≤ 45 µm) in equiatomic proportions, cold‑pressing to 65 % theoretical density, and consolidating in a spark‑plasma‑sintering furnace under a 50 MPa load at 1350 °C for five minutes before furnace cooling. Rectangular specimens were machined with a single‑edge V‑notch of varying root radius to probe notch sensitivity, and compression tests were performed at room temperature at a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. The as‑sintered microstructure displayed a homogeneous BCC matrix with occasional submicron Hf‑rich precipitates along grain boundaries; grain size remained in the sub‑micron regime, and residual porosity was below 2 %. Compression curves revealed a sharp elastic‑to‑plastic transition followed by limited strain hardening, indicating low ductility typical of brittle BCC HEAs. Samples with sharper notches exhibited earlier onset of localized cracking and a pronounced reduction in apparent fracture resistance, confirming high notch sensitivity; broader notches retained a larger plastic zone and displayed marginally higher effective fracture toughness. These observations underscore that in TaVZrWHf the combination of limited dislocation mobility, strong lattice distortion, and the presence of brittle intermetallic clusters governs both the yield response and the pronounced susceptibility of the material to notch‑induced fracture.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: The TiZrHf refractory high‑entropy alloy was fabricated by blending elemental powders of Ti, Zr, and Hf in equiatomic proportions, followed by mechanical alloying for several hours to achieve a homogeneous nanocrystalline mixture; subsequent spark plasma sintering was performed under a uniaxial load of several tens of MPa at temperatures just below the alloy’s solidus, with a rapid heating rate to limit grain growth. Optical microscopy and electron back‑scatter diffraction revealed a predominately body‑centered cubic matrix with a modest fraction of elongated grain clusters aligned parallel to the loading axis, while transmission electron microscopy identified a high density of dislocation loops and nanoscale Hf‑rich precipitates at grain boundaries. Fatigue testing in tension–tension loading showed that crack initiation preferentially occurred at the interfaces between these precipitate‑enriched boundaries and the surrounding matrix, where local strain concentration was amplified by lattice mismatch. Once a microcrack formed, propagation proceeded along a tortuous path that repeatedly intersected high‑angle grain boundaries, causing frequent crack tip blunting and intermittent crack arrest. The observed retardation of crack advance correlated with the fine grain size and the dispersed secondary phase particles, both of which contribute to a higher fatigue threshold by promoting crack tip shielding and increasing the effective crack closure ratio.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy WVZr, consolidated by powder metallurgy and spark‑plasma sintering, exhibits a simple body‑centered cubic matrix that can be leveraged as a durable substrate for high‑temperature protective coatings. The rapid densification inherent to SPS yields a fine, equiaxed grain structure with limited residual porosity, which promotes strong metallurgical bonding to ceramic overlay layers such as Al₂O₃, TiAlN or SiC‑based composites. Solid‑solution strengthening from the large atomic size mismatch between W, V, and Zr contributes to a high intrinsic oxidation resistance, while the modest lattice distortion facilitates diffusion pathways that aid in the formation of a thin, adherent oxide scale during service. Tailoring the surface finish—through controlled polishing or plasma‑etching—enhances nucleation of the coating and reduces interfacial stress concentrations, thereby improving crack‑propagation resistance under cyclic thermal loading. The combined effect of a refined microstructure, low porosity, and compatible thermal expansion between WVZr and the selected coating material underpins the alloy’s suitability for protective applications in extreme environments.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: high-temperature coating or surface protection strategies

text: The laser‑directed energy deposition of the ternary refractory system TaMoHf yields a dense, columnar microstructure in which the measured Vickers microhardness is uniformly elevated across all indents, indicating a consistently stiff response throughout the build. This high hardness correlates with an unusually large elastic modulus, a consequence of the predominance of metallic‑covalent bonding contributed by the d‑electron overlap of Ta and Mo combined with the modestly higher electronegativity of Hf, which together enhance lattice rigidity. The absence of pronounced compositional segregation in the DED tracks ensures that the solid‑solution strengthening from the size mismatch among Ta, Mo, and Hf atoms is uniformly distributed, reinforcing the lattice and raising the modulus without the need for secondary phases. Moreover, the rapid cooling inherent to the process refines the grain size, further restricting dislocation motion and amplifying the bond‑controlled stiffness, a trend that is reflected by the consistently high Vickers hardness readings across the examined locations.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy TaHfWReMoNb, when consolidated by powder metallurgy and spark‑plasma sintering, undergoes a recrystallization sequence that is strongly dictated by its extreme lattice distortion and the wide distribution of melting points among the constituent elements. During the rapid heating pulse of SPS, recovery of the heavily cold‑worked powder particles is initiated by the annihilation of dislocation tangles, but the high configurational entropy delays the nucleation of new strain‑free grains until the temperature approaches the upper third of the sintering range. Once nuclei form, the severe solid‑solution strengthening provided by the Ta‑Hf‑W‑Re‑Mo‑Nb matrix slows boundary migration, so grain growth proceeds sluggishly and often displays a pinning effect from residual oxide inclusions that survived the powder‑mixing stage. Fine‑grained microstructures are therefore retained even after prolonged holds, whereas coarser grains tend to appear only in regions where local compositional fluctuations reduce lattice strain, allowing the grain‑boundary energy to dominate the kinetic driving force.

text: In the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaMoZrTiWV produced by vacuum‑induction melting, the crystallographic texture that inevitably develops during additive‑manufacturing or directional solidification can dominate the tensile response at elevated temperature. When the columnar grains align their <100> axes parallel to the build direction, the high‑temperature flow stress measured along that axis tends to be higher than in directions intersecting the {110} or {111} families, reflecting the anisotropic slip‑system activity of the body‑centered cubic matrix. Conversely, samples whose grains are rotated toward a random orientation display a more isotropic curve, with lower peak stresses but greater uniform elongation because multiple slip systems are simultaneously recruited. The controlled‑atmosphere furnace suppresses oxidation, allowing the intrinsic texture‑controlled hardening to be isolated from surface embrittlement. Grain‑boundary cohesion, solid‑solution distortion from the five constituent elements, and the modest presence of sub‑micron carbides further modulate the anisotropy, with finer, well‑aligned grains amplifying directional strength while coarser, misoriented grains promote ductility across all loading axes.

text: During suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrReHfW, a 50‑mm diameter ingot was formed under a 1‑atm argon atmosphere to suppress oxidation of the reactive Zr and Hf constituents. The rapid solidification rate of ~10⁵ K s⁻¹ produced a dendritic microstructure with primary dendrite arm spacings of 12–15 µm. Subsequent grinding and polishing revealed a network of sub‑micron pores, predominantly located along interdendritic regions where the Re‑rich liquid solidified last. Rockwell hardness measurements, carried out at H2 load, indicated a mean hardness of 520 HRB with a standard deviation of ±25 HRB, while localized hardness dips correlated strongly with porosity clusters. These voids act as stress concentrators during cyclic loading, reducing fracture toughness by promoting crack initiation at the pore tips and limiting crack‑closure mechanisms. Fatigue tests performed to 10⁶ cycles at 1 % strain amplitude revealed a reduction in life by approximately 30 % compared to cast samples with <0.1 vol % porosity, underscoring the sensitivity of ZrReHfW to processing‑induced defects.

text: Mechanical alloying of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WNbVTi followed by hot pressing yielded dense, nanocrystalline bulk specimens with average grain sizes below 200 nm. Compact‑tension specimens exhibited a high critical stress intensity factor but a markedly lower fatigue crack initiation life than conventional wrought alloys. Fractography revealed that cracks preferentially nucleated at elongated intergranular pores and at secondary Ti‑rich lamellae, suggesting that local stress concentrators arising from compositional heterogeneity are the dominant initiation sites. During subsequent crack growth, the fine, heavily distorted lattice of WNbVTi produced a pronounced lattice‑distortion strengthening effect, leading to a steep crack‑velocity gradient and a relatively low crack‑growth rate for stress intensity factors above the threshold. The interplay between solid‑solution strengthening, grain‑boundary pinning, and the presence of nanoscale Ti‑rich precipitates resulted in a fatigue limit that is high for its density but limited by the propensity for intergranular decohesion at high cycling stresses. Overall, the fatigue life of WNbVTi is governed by the balance between grain‑size‑controlled toughness and the susceptibility of interfacial regions to crack initiation.

subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life

text: The refractory alloy TaMoHfRe belongs to the class of high‑entropy systems because its constituent elements are present in near‑equiatomic proportions, which maximizes configurational entropy and stabilizes a single‑phase solid solution at elevated temperatures. During mechanical alloying, repeated fracturing and cold welding create a highly mixed powder whose enthalpy of mixing is modestly negative; the relatively small magnitude of the binary interaction parameters for Ta–Mo, Mo–Hf, Hf–Re and the other pairs prevents deep exothermic driving forces that would otherwise favor intermetallic segregation. Consequently, the Gibbs free energy curve is dominated by the entropy term, allowing the body‑centered cubic lattice to persist through hot pressing. Valence‑electron concentration (VEC) in this alloy hovers near the threshold that favors BCC stability, as each element contributes a comparable number of d‑electrons; this VEC balance suppresses the formation of ordered compounds and promotes a chemically disordered matrix. The combined effect of high configurational entropy, limited negative mixing enthalpy, and an optimal VEC therefore dictates the thermodynamic pathway that leads to a single‑phase refractory HEA after consolidation.

text: A refractory high entropy alloy composed of TaNbVReMoZr was synthesized by suction casting within an argon‑purged chamber to suppress oxidation and ensure a uniform microstructure. The resulting alloy exhibited a dense, single‑phase bcc matrix with nanometer‑scale coherent precipitates of (Mo,Re) rich sub‑lamellae. Cyclic tensile–tensile testing revealed a fatigue life that decreases sharply with increasing mean stress, yet remains substantially higher than conventional bcc alloys of similar composition. Detailed crack initiation studies indicated that micro‑cracks preferentially form at sites of localized lattice distortion, where the large atomic size mismatch between Ta and V induces dislocation pile‑ups. Subsequent crack propagation proceeds through a mixed mode of intergranular and transgranular fracture; the fine secondary precipitates impede crack advance by acting as obstacle pinning points, effectively increasing the crack‑tip shielding. Consequently, the alloy’s fatigue endurance is governed by the synergy between solid solution strengthening, the high density of coherent nanoscale precipitates, and the suppression of porosity during rapid solidification, underscoring the critical role of processing‑controlled microstructure in tailoring fatigue performance.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy MoCrTaWVHf fabricated by vacuum‑induction melting and subsequently shaped by directed energy deposition exhibits pronounced tensile anisotropy that correlates with the microstructural texture imparted during layer‑wise solidification. Nano‑indentation arrays performed on cross‑sections reveal a systematic variation of hardness and elastic modulus that aligns with the elongated columnar grains and the intergranular network of BCC‑type solid‑solution matrix interspersed with nanoscale Hf‑rich precipitates. Regions oriented parallel to the build direction display elevated hardness and modulus, reflecting enhanced lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening along the <001> texture, whereas transverse sections show comparatively lower values where grain boundaries and residual porosity are more prevalent. The disparity in local mechanical response translates into direction‑dependent tensile strength and ductility, with the build‑axis samples sustaining higher loads but lower elongation, while off‑axis specimens demonstrate more uniform strain distribution. These findings underscore the critical role of texture‑controlled microstructural heterogeneity in governing anisotropic tensile behavior of additively manufactured MoCrTaWVHf.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: The CrHfMoReTiTaV alloy was synthesized by repeated arc‑melting of high‑purity elements under a Ti getter atmosphere, each melt being inverted and re‑remelted to ensure chemical homogeneity before the liquid was drop‑cast into a copper chill block to obtain cylindrical billets. Sections were subsequently extracted parallel and perpendicular to the solidification direction and subjected to uniaxial tension according to ASTM E8, employing a strain‑rate consistent with standard practice and extensometer‑based deformation measurement. Tensile curves revealed a pronounced directional dependence: specimens loaded along the casting axis exhibited a higher flow stress and delayed necking compared with those loaded transverse to the columnar dendrite alignment. Metallographic examination showed elongated grains and a strong <001> texture in the longitudinal direction, while the transverse sections displayed a more equiaxed grain morphology with weaker texture. The observed anisotropy is attributed to the combined effects of grain shape anisotropy, crystallographic texture, and the segregation of refractory solutes along dendritic cores, which collectively elevate dislocation resistance when the loading axis aligns with the preferred slip systems.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting

text: CrHfMoTiZrWTa and VWTiNbMoHf are both synthesized by suction casting in an argon‑protected environment, ensuring negligible oxygen uptake and promoting a fine, equiaxed microstructure. In CrHfMoTiZrWTa, the presence of Cr and Zr leads to the precipitation of intermetallic σ‑phase and κ‑phase particles during rapid solidification, which locally obstruct dislocation motion and enhance hardness. The relative proportion of these hard, brittle phases is elevated because Cr and Zr possess larger atomic radii and form stable compounds with Mo and W. Conversely, VWTiNbMoHf contains V and Nb, whose smaller size mismatch with Mo and W reduces the tendency to form secondary intermetallics; instead, a supersaturated solid solution dominates, providing moderate solid‑solution strengthening but fewer hard precipitates. Consequently, CrHfMoTiZrWTa is expected to exhibit higher hardness than VWTiNbMoHf, mainly due to its richer secondary phase content, while the latter’s hardness remains governed mainly by lattice distortion and solid‑solution effects.

text: In powder‑metallurgy routes such as spark‑plasma sintering, the balance between a solid‑solution matrix and any secondary intermetallics strongly dictates the hardness of refractory high‑entropy alloys. In MoHfCr, the large atomic size mismatch between Mo and Hf promotes extensive lattice distortion, yet the thermodynamic driving force for Hf‑rich Laves‑phase or HfCr₂ precipitates is relatively modest; consequently the microstructure typically retains a predominantly single‑phase BCC matrix with only a sparse distribution of fine, incoherent particles. These few precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation glide, but their limited volume fraction means the hardness is governed chiefly by solid‑solution strengthening. By contrast, TiNbMoCr lies closer to the compositional valley where Ti and Cr readily combine to form Cr‑rich silicide‑type or TiCr₂ precipitates that nucleate along grain boundaries and within grains during SPS cooling. The resulting higher volume fraction of coherent or semi‑coherent second phases provides additional pinning of dislocations and grain‑boundary strengthening, pushing the overall hardness above that of MoHfCr. Thus, all else being equal, the TiNbMoCr alloy is expected to exhibit a modestly higher hardness because its richer precipitate content contributes more effectively to resistance against plastic deformation.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: The VZrReCrMoWHf alloy was built layer‑by‑layer in a directed‑energy‑deposition system using a 1 kW fiber laser under an argon shield, with a nominal composition of equiatomic V, Zr, Re, Cr, Mo, W, and Hf. After deposition, rectangular coupons (10 × 5 × 2 mm) were extracted by wire EDM and surface‑ground to a finish below 0.2 µm Ra before resonant ultrasound spectroscopy (RUS) measurements. The RUS spectra revealed a set of well‑separated resonances that could be fitted to an orthotropic elastic model, yielding an average Young’s modulus that was systematically higher than that of binary refractory alloys of comparable density. The increase was attributed to the pronounced covalent‑metallic bonding contributed by the high‑valence d‑electron elements (Re, W, Mo) and the modest lattice distortion introduced by the large‑radius Hf and Zr atoms, which together stiffen the electron cloud without generating excessive internal stress. Samples with a finer, columnar dendrite spacing—resulting from a reduced laser scan speed—showed a modest upward shift in the modulus, consistent with the reduced compliance of the denser, more uniformly bonded microstructure.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy HfTaVCr, fabricated by powder metallurgy followed by spark‑plasma sintering, exemplifies the tendency of multicomponent systems to adopt a body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution when the constituent elements share similar atomic radii and crystal structures. During high‑energy ball‑milling, the elemental powders become intimately mixed, and the subsequent rapid heating in the spark‑plasma furnace promotes atomic diffusion while maintaining a short dwell time, thereby limiting the growth of secondary phases. The resulting microstructure is dominated by a single BCC phase with a lattice parameter that lies between those of the pure elements, indicating successful substitutional solid‑solution formation. The high lattice distortion introduced by the wide range of atomic sizes and the strong bonding character of the refractory elements suppress the segregation of intermetallic compounds, thereby stabilizing the solid solution across a broad temperature range. The absence of pronounced secondary phases and the uniform distribution of solute atoms contribute to enhanced thermodynamic stability and a relatively low driving force for phase decomposition, which is crucial for high‑temperature structural applications.

subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy WReCrMoTi, produced by vacuum‑induction melting followed by homogenization at elevated temperature, exhibits a fatigue response governed by its complex BCC matrix and the distribution of nanoscale compositional fluctuations. Electron‑probe mapping reveals modest segregation of Re and Cr along interdendritic channels, generating localized elastic‑modulus mismatches that serve as preferential sites for crack nucleation under cyclic loading. Grain‑size refinement achieved through controlled cooling promotes a higher density of high‑angle grain boundaries, which act as barriers to early crack advance but also concentrate slip bands that can accelerate crack growth once a critical dislocation pile‑up forms. The presence of dispersed, coherent W‑rich precipitates impedes dislocation motion, raising the threshold stress intensity for crack propagation, while residual porosity, even at sub‑percent levels, provides micro‑voids that coalesce into secondary cracks under high‑R ratio cycles. Collectively, these microstructural features—interdendritic segregation, grain‑boundary character, precipitate spacing, and minimal porosity—dictate the alloy’s fatigue crack initiation sites, propagation rates, and ultimately its fatigue life.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: fatigue crack initiation and propagation behavior, and features that influence fatigue life

text: The VWZrMoHfNb alloy was prepared by vacuum‑induction melting of the constituent elements (99.99 % purity) under a 10‑5 torr argon atmosphere, followed by drop‑casting into a copper chill mold to obtain 20 mm‑thick plates. After homogenization at 1500 °C for 24 h, the surface was mechanically polished to a 1 µm finish and subsequently subjected to three distinct high‑temperature protection schemes. In the first route, a 5‑µm Al2O3‑based ceramic coating was deposited by atmospheric plasma spraying; the coating adhered uniformly and displayed limited spallation after exposure to 1200 °C for 100 h, indicating that the residual thermal expansion mismatch was partially mitigated by the fine lamellar microstructure of the splats. The second approach employed pack cementation of a MoSi2 diffusion barrier, which penetrated several micrometres into the alloy and formed a graded Mo‑Si‑O interlayer that suppressed oxidation by limiting oxygen ingress to the underlying matrix. Finally, a thin (≈200 nm) TiAlN nitride film was grown by reactive magnetron sputtering at 600 °C; the dense columnar grains of the nitride resisted catastrophic cracking during cyclic heating to 1100 °C, and energy‑dispersive X‑ray mapping revealed a diffusion‑free interface. Across all treatments, the underlying BCC solid‑solution retained its dendritic‑cellular morphology, while the protective layers altered the surface roughness and residual stress state, factors that will be correlated with subsequent high‑temperature wear and oxidation tests.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: high-temperature coating or surface protection strategies

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy WVZrMoTa was synthesized by vacuum arc melting and rapid solidification through drop casting, producing a heavily textured, dendritic as‑cast microstructure with compositional fluctuations at the sub‑micron scale. Subsequent homogenization at elevated temperature promoted extensive solute diffusion, eliminating segregation bands and fostering a more uniform body‑centered cubic solid solution enriched in the refractory constituents. Grain coarsening accompanied the reduction of high‑angle boundaries, while the dissolution of residual intermetallic clusters yielded a single‑phase microstructure characterized by pronounced lattice distortion and increased solid‑solution strengthening. Transmission electron microscopy revealed the disappearance of nanoscale precipitates that previously acted as obstacles to dislocation motion, and atom probe analyses confirmed the approach to equiatomic composition throughout the bulk. The annealed state thus displays a refined balance between enhanced ductility, derived from reduced internal stresses, and maintained high-temperature strength due to the retained distortion of the refractory matrix.

text: The refractory alloy Ta‑Hf‑W‑Re‑Mo‑Nb, fabricated by mechanical alloying of elemental powders followed by spark‑plasma sintering, exhibits a recrystallization pathway that is strongly governed by its severe lattice distortion and the high melting points of its constituent elements. During the rapid thermal pulse of SPS, a dense, sub‑micron microstructure forms in which dislocation tangles and deformation‑induced sub‑grains are trapped at compositional fluctuation boundaries; these act as nucleation sites for new, strain‑free grains once the temperature exceeds the onset of recrystallization. Because each element contributes a comparable atomic fraction, the stored energy is distributed uniformly, leading to a relatively broad nucleation window rather than a sharp burst. Grain growth thereafter proceeds sluggishly, as the high degree of solid‑solution strengthening and the presence of nanoscale precipitates—often rich in Hf and Nb—impede boundary migration. Consequently, grain coarsening follows a diffusion‑controlled kinetic law with an exponent that reflects the combined effects of sluggish diffusion in the refractory matrix and pinning by second‑phase particles, yielding a microstructure that remains fine even after extended high‑temperature exposure.

text: Powder‑metallurgy routes were employed to fabricate VWHfTiCrMoTa and TiVHfZrMo, each comprising equiatomic mixtures of the respective refractory elements. After ball‑mill grinding, powders were pre‑compacted and subjected to spark‑plasma sintering at 2000 °C under 50 MPa, yielding dense bulk specimens with porosities below 2 %. Compression tests performed at room temperature revealed a pronounced asymmetry between tensile and compressive yielding: the VWHfTiCrMoTa alloy displayed a higher compressive yield stress compared to its tensile counterpart, a trend attributable to its finer, more homogeneously distributed secondary TiH₂ precipitates that impede dislocation motion preferentially in the compression regime. Conversely, TiVHfZrMo exhibited a comparatively lower compressive yield response, correlating with its coarser Zr‑rich intermetallic clusters that act as weak planes under compressive loading. Grain size refinement during sintering further amplified these effects, with the VWHfTiCrMoTa alloy maintaining a finer microstructure due to the stabilizing influence of Cr, whereas TiVHfZrMo experienced slight grain growth from the Zr‑Zr bonding network. Overall, the microstructural heterogeneities and phase distribution inherent to each composition dictate the observed compressive yield asymmetry.

text: Both VZrHfReTaCrW and WMoReNbTaHf were fabricated by identical powder metallurgy routes followed by spark plasma sintering, ensuring comparable densification and residual porosity. In VZrHfReTaCrW the high fraction of Zr and Hf, both with large atomic radii, imposes significant lattice distortion, enhancing solid‑solution strengthening relative to WMoReNbTaHf, which contains more transition metals with smaller size mismatches. The presence of V and Cr in the first alloy also promotes a more complex solid solution, further impeding dislocation motion. Grain size evolution during sintering is largely controlled by the sintering temperature and dwell time; the VZrHfReTaCrW matrix tends to retain a finer microstructure because the Zr/Hf network acts as a barrier to grain growth, whereas the W‑rich matrix in WMoReNbTaHf exhibits slightly coarser grains. Consequently, the VZrHfReTaCrW alloy is expected to display a higher tensile strength at room temperature, while the WMoReNbTaHf alloy may achieve a modestly lower strength but potentially better ductility due to its finer lattice distortion and more uniform grain boundary cohesion.

text: The HfZrVNbRe refractory high‑entropy alloy produced by high‑energy mechanical alloying and subsequently hot‑pressed to near‑full density exhibits a pronounced dependence of yield strength on the degree of solid‑solution strengthening imparted by the five constituent refractory elements. Microstructural examination reveals a single‑phase BCC matrix in which severe lattice distortion arises from the substantial size mismatch among Hf, Zr, V, Nb and Re, generating high internal stress fields that impede dislocation glide. As the hot‑pressing schedule is tuned to increase solute homogenization, the lattice parameter distribution narrows, and the resultant rise in configurational entropy further locks dislocations, elevating the yield strength observed in the compact‑tension specimens. Fracture‑toughness tests show that samples with the highest solute disorder sustain larger crack‑tip opening displacements before yielding, indicating that the same solid‑solution mechanisms that raise the flow stress also contribute to a modestly tougher response, whereas reductions in lattice distortion through partial segregation diminish both yield strength and the associated resistance to crack initiation.

text: The fracture‑toughness response of brittle BCC‑type refractory high‑entropy alloys is governed primarily by the ease with which a crack tip can be blunted by dislocation activity or by the presence of toughening micro‑features, and this sensitivity is amplified in notched specimens where stress concentration is extreme. In the six‑component system VZrTiWMoCrTa, the large lattice‑distortion field created by the combination of five high‑melting‑point transition metals and the relatively low‑modulus Zr and Ti promotes strong solid‑solution strengthening, but it also suppresses the nucleation of mobile dislocations, leaving the material highly notch‑sensitive; any crack tip that encounters a region of high local strain energy will propagate with little resistance, yielding a comparatively low fracture‑toughness trend. By contrast, the simpler ZrVWCr alloy contains fewer elements that generate severe lattice strain, and the presence of Zr and Cr can foster a modest amount of ductile‑phase segregation or nanoscale precipitates along grain boundaries during rapid laser‑induced solidification. These features can act as crack‑tip arrest sites, reducing notch sensitivity and allowing limited plastic shielding, so ZrVWCr is expected to exhibit a higher fracture‑toughness in notched tests despite its overall brittle BCC matrix.

text: The VTaCrTiNb refractory high‑entropy alloy, fabricated by blending elemental powders, compacting, and spark‑plasma‑sintering (SPS) at temperatures just below its solidus, exhibits a single‑phase body‑centered cubic matrix whose yield strength is dominated by solid‑solution hardening. Tensile specimens prepared according to ASTM E8 reveal that the rapid heating and short dwell of SPS suppress grain growth, yielding sub‑micron grains whose contribution to strength is modest compared with the lattice‑distortion effect of five near‑equiatomic constituents. Each solute atom introduces a size mismatch and differing modulus relative to the average matrix, generating a high configurational entropy that impedes dislocation motion through a forest of local strain fields. As the Cr and Ti fractions increase, the mismatch between their smaller atomic radii and the larger V and Nb atoms intensifies, raising the yield stress, whereas modest additions of Ta, whose modulus is comparable to the matrix, provide a smaller incremental boost. Conversely, any residual porosity introduced during powder consolidation acts as a stress concentrator, locally reducing the measured yield point; thus, densification levels achieved by optimizing SPS pressure and current directly modulate the apparent strength. Overall, the observed trend—higher yield strength with greater atomic‑size disparity and reduced porosity—reflects the primary role of solid‑solution strengthening in this refractory HEA.

text: Mechanical alloying of MoZrCrTi and TiVReHfTaCrNb followed by hot‑pressing produced bulk BCC high‑entropy alloys with dense, fine‑grained microstructures. The MoZrCrTi alloy, containing a larger fraction of early transition metals with higher lattice distortion, exhibits a more pronounced grain‑size‑controlled fracture process; its lower average grain size promotes higher fracture toughness by constraining crack advance and enhancing energy dissipation through grain‑boundary sliding. In contrast, TiVReHfTaCrNb possesses a higher overall valence electron concentration and a more extensive presence of refractory elements that stabilize a harder, more brittle BCC lattice, resulting in greater notch sensitivity. The larger atomic size mismatch and reduced dislocation mobility in TiVReHfTaCrNb limit plastic work ahead of a notch, thereby lowering its fracture toughness relative to MoZrCrTi. Thus, notch‑sensitive behaviour and fracture toughness are expected to be higher in the MoZrCrTi alloy, while TiVReHfTaCrNb should show comparatively lower toughness due to its intrinsically brittle BCC microstructure.

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy ReHfZrCrTi in an inert argon atmosphere yields a near‑equiatomic solid solution with limited intermetallic segregation, a microstructure characterized by ultrafine equiaxed grains and a modest amount of fine Re‑rich secondary phases. Rockwell hardness measurements reveal a high baseline hardness and a pronounced hardening gradient near the surface, indicative of surface‑induced compressive stresses and residual strain from the casting process. These hardness gradients correlate with the initiation of fatigue cracks; the harder near‑surface region promotes localized plastic strain under cyclic loading, while the surrounding softer matrix facilitates the formation of micro‑cracks. During propagation, the fine grain structure impedes dislocation motion, creating a tortuous path that increases crack tip shielding. However, the presence of Re‑rich precipitates can act as stress concentrators if their spacing is insufficiently large, accelerating crack growth. Overall, the combination of high hardness, fine grain size, and controlled secondary phase distribution defines a fatigue life that is sensitive to surface finish and residual stress state, with smoother surfaces and lower residual tensile stresses yielding the longest crack‑life extensions.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy HfNbTi, synthesized by blending elemental powders, compacting them, and consolidating the green body through spark‑plasma sintering, displays a tensile response that is strongly linked to its temperature‑dependent microstructure. At cryogenic and room temperatures the alloy retains a single‑phase body‑centered‑cubic solid solution, and the pronounced lattice distortion produced by the size mismatch among Hf, Nb and Ti generates substantial solid‑solution strengthening, giving rise to a high yield strength that remains close to the ultimate tensile strength. As the temperature rises toward the intermediate range (several hundred degrees Celsius), thermally activated dislocation glide becomes easier; the yield point drops more rapidly than the ultimate strength because the high‑temperature recovery processes diminish the effectiveness of lattice distortion while the inherent strength of the solid solution still sustains a respectable ultimate load. Near the alloy’s recrystallization onset, grain growth and the possible formation of minor secondary phases further soften the material, causing both tensile and yield strengths to converge toward lower values, yet the overall temperature trend remains a gradual decline rather than an abrupt loss of load‑bearing capacity.

text: The refractory alloy WReCrVZr synthesized by powder metallurgy and consolidated through spark‑plasma sintering displays a pronounced hardness gradient that correlates with the evolving secondary‑phase population as the elemental ratios are altered. When the Re and Cr fractions are increased relative to V and Zr, the high‑entropy matrix retains a body‑centered cubic lattice but a greater volume fraction of intermetallic precipitates—primarily W‑rich Laves‑type and Cr‑Zr carbides—appears along grain boundaries and within the grains. These hard, stoichiometric inclusions act as formidable obstacles to dislocation glide, thereby raising the overall Vickers response, whereas compositions richer in V and Zr tend to suppress precipitate nucleation, yielding a softer, more ductile microstructure dominated by a single‑phase solid solution. Moreover, finer sintered powders promote a uniform distribution of nano‑scale precipitates, amplifying the hardening effect, while excessive porosity in under‑sintered samples diminishes load transfer and reduces hardness despite comparable phase fractions.

text: A refractory high‑entropy alloy composed of W, Zr, Ti, Cr, Mo, and Nb was synthesized by vacuum induction melting followed by homogenization at 1900 °C. Microstructural analysis revealed a single BCC solid solution with slight Zr‑rich enrichment at grain boundaries. Elastic modulus measurements across the series of equiatomic compositions indicated a pronounced increase as the tungsten content rose, reflecting the strong covalent‑metallic bonding associated with W's high valence electron concentration. Conversely, alloying with Zr and Ti, which possess larger atomic radii and more pronounced d‑band overlap, led to a slight softening of the lattice, thereby reducing Young’s modulus. The observed trend aligns with lattice distortion models where the average atomic size mismatch and electronic density of states jointly modulate the elastic response: the heavier, more compact W atoms enhance stiffness, while the larger Zr/Ti atoms introduce localized lattice strain that lowers the overall modulus. This systematic compositional tuning offers a pathway to tailor stiffness in refractory HEAs for high‑temperature structural applications.

text: The tensile response of laser‑directed energy deposition (DED) alloys MoTiZrV and VMoWReNbHfZr was examined with respect to build‑direction anisotropy, revealing contrasting trends rooted in their compositional complexity and resulting microstructures. In the simpler MoTiZrV system, rapid solidification produces a relatively uniform body‑centered cubic matrix with modest lattice distortion, allowing columnar grains to align with the thermal gradient; this texture promotes higher longitudinal strength but modest transverse softening, yielding a pronounced anisotropy. By contrast, the multicomponent VMoWReNbHfZr alloy exhibits pronounced elemental partitioning during solidification, generating a fine dispersion of refractory‑rich precipitates and a more pronounced crystallographic texture that is partially randomized by the presence of Hf‑ and Zr‑rich oxide inclusions. Consequently, the longitudinal tensile strength remains competitive, yet the transverse direction retains a larger fraction of the load‑bearing capacity, reducing overall anisotropy. The combined effects of solid‑solution strengthening, precipitate spacing, and grain‑orientation distribution thus predict that VMoWReNbHfZr will display a comparatively lower directional disparity than MoTiZrV.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy HfTaVCr, when consolidated by powder metallurgy followed by spark‑plasma sintering, typically evolves a single‑phase body‑centered‑cubic (BCC) solid solution because the constituent elements share comparable atomic sizes and high melting points that suppress the formation of intermetallic compounds during rapid heating and cooling. The high configurational entropy associated with five principal elements lowers the Gibbs free energy of the mixed state, stabilizing the BCC lattice against ordering, while the strong mutual solubility of Hf, Ta, V, and Cr on the BCC sublattice promotes a homogeneous distribution of atoms. The rapid heating rates in SPS limit diffusion pathways, preventing the segregation of Cr‑rich or V‑rich clusters that might otherwise nucleate secondary phases. Nevertheless, slight compositional fluctuations can arise at grain boundaries, where residual porosity or oxide films act as nucleation sites for minor carbide or nitride precipitates; these are typically sparse enough not to disrupt the overall BCC matrix but can modestly influence local mechanical response.

text: Arc‑melted refractory high‑entropy alloys MoVTaReCrNb and VWTaCrZrReMo were drop‑cast to form near‑equiatomic compositions, and their elongation at fracture was investigated in comparison. The MoVTaReCrNb alloy displays a more uniform, fine‑grained microstructure with limited intermetallic phase formation, a characteristic that typically supports higher ductility through grain‑boundary sliding and reduced stress concentration. In contrast, VWTaCrZrReMo contains a higher volume fraction of coherent precipitates such as V₂Ta and ReZr intermetallics, which, while strengthening the matrix, can act as nucleation sites for voids and crack initiation during tensile deformation. The presence of these secondary phases also impedes the motion of dislocations, increasing the likelihood of localized shear banding. Consequently, the MoVTaReCrNb alloy is expected to exhibit a comparatively larger elongation at fracture, whereas VWTaCrZrReMo would tend toward lower ductility due to its more pronounced precipitate‑induced brittleness.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy VNbZrWMoHf was synthesized by vacuum‑induction melting followed by rapid solidification, yielding a predominantly body‑centered cubic matrix that is heavily supersaturated with the constituent transition metals. Subsequent annealing at intermediate temperatures promoted the nucleation of Laves‑type compounds, principally V‑rich (V,Zr)₂(Nb,Mo) and Hf‑containing C14‑type phases, which were observed to segregate along grain boundaries and within the interior of grains as finely dispersed platelets. The volume fraction and morphology of these intermetallics were strongly dependent on the aging schedule; longer holds at 1200 °C produced coarser, more contiguous Laves networks, whereas short‑duration treatments at 1000 °C retained a uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates. Transmission‑electron microscopy revealed coherent interfaces between the matrix and the early‑stage precipitates, suggesting that lattice misfit strain contributes to the observed strengthening, while the later‑stage coarsening reduces barrier effectiveness. The balance between precipitation strengthening and potential embrittlement from continuous Laves films is discussed in terms of thermodynamic driving forces and diffusion kinetics intrinsic to the VNbZrWMoHf system.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy WZrTiCrMoNb synthesized by vacuum‑induction melting exhibits a markedly elevated Young’s modulus that can be rationalized through its constituent bonding hierarchy and lattice chemistry. The predominance of early‑transition metals (W, Mo, Nb) contributes extensive d‑orbital overlap, fostering a high degree of metallic covalency that stiffens the crystal lattice, while the addition of Zr and Ti introduces moderate s‑p hybridization, subtly reducing the overall bond polarity but preserving rigidity. First‑principles calculations suggest that the average valence electron concentration and the resulting bulk modulus scale positively with the proportion of high‑elastic‑modulus elements, a trend corroborated by ultrasonic measurements showing a systematic increase relative to binary refractory counterparts. Moreover, the single‑phase BCC structure retained after melting and solidification minimizes grain‑boundary compliance, allowing the intrinsic bond stiffness to dominate the macroscopic elastic response. This compositional‑bonding framework provides a predictive basis for tailoring elastic performance in other multi‑principal refractory systems.

text: The directed‑energy deposition routes produced a columnar‑like microstructure in both VHfZrMo and the more complex NbReWCrZrMoV, yet the two chemistries diverge in the balance of lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening that governs their tensile response. In the ternary‑dominant VHfZrMo, the high atomic‑size mismatch among V, Hf and Zr generates pronounced lattice strain, which together with a relatively coarse columnar grain morphology yields a moderate yield plateau but a rapid strain hardening rate as dislocations interact with the distorted lattice. By contrast, NbReWCrZrMoV incorporates five additional refractory elements that increase the overall valence electron concentration and promote a finer, equiaxed grain refinement during rapid solidification; the dense mixture of Nb, Re, W, Cr, Mo and V amplifies solid‑solution strengthening while also introducing a dispersed network of nano‑scale intermetallic clusters that act as effective barriers to dislocation motion. Consequently, the Nb‑based alloy is expected to exhibit a higher ultimate tensile strength and a more gradual work‑hardening slope than VHfZrMo, even though its larger compositional complexity can modestly reduce ductility relative to the simpler V‑Hf‑Zr‑Mo system.

text: The laser‑directed energy deposition of HfNbCrZrVMoW produces a columnar dendritic texture in which the primary grain width varies markedly with scan strategy and heat‑input parameters, providing a natural laboratory for Hall‑Petch analysis. Extensometer traces recorded during monotonic tension reveal that specimens with finer equiaxed grains exhibit a steeper initial slope of the load‑extension curve, indicating a higher true stress at comparable true strain and consequently a higher apparent yield strength. Simultaneously, the measured elastic‑recovery segment shortens, reflecting an increase in lattice resistance that translates into greater indentation resistance; micro‑hardness mappings show a systematic rise as the average grain diameter is reduced. The data suggest that grain‑boundary strengthening dominates over the modest contribution from solid‑solution effects in this alloy, because the dislocation pile‑up length scales inversely with grain size, raising both the flow stress and the hardness. In contrast, coarse‑grained deposits display extended uniform elongation before necking, confirming the classic trade‑off between grain‑refinement‑driven strength and ductility in this refractory high‑entropy system.

text: ReHfNbVWZr is a five‑component refractory high‑entropy alloy whose body‑centered cubic lattice accommodates a large degree of atomic size mismatch, generating pronounced lattice distortion that governs its mechanical response. When the alloy is prepared by arc melting and subsequently drop‑cast, rapid solidification produces a columnar grain texture aligned with the heat flow direction; in additively manufactured builds this texture is further amplified by the layer‑wise thermal gradient. Consequently, tensile behavior becomes directionally dependent: loading parallel to the columnar axis engages well‑aligned slip systems and typically yields higher ductility and lower flow stress, whereas loading transverse to the texture forces dislocations to negotiate a higher density of grain boundaries and crystallographic misorientations, raising the apparent yield strength and reducing elongation. The anisotropy is also accentuated by residual stress fields that develop during solidification and layer deposition, and by the segregation of refractory elements such as V and W to grain‑boundary regions, which stiffens those interfaces. Understanding how the interplay of texture, lattice distortion, and element partitioning shapes the directional tensile response is essential for tailoring ReHfNbVWZr components for high‑temperature load‑bearing applications.

In contrast, the VZrHfReTaCrW alloy, while still highly distorted, contains fewer heavy, high‑melting‑point elements and its grain size after SPS is often coarser due to lower sintering temperatures required to avoid volatilization of V. text: The TiVWTaZrMo refractory high‑entropy alloy produced by intensive mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot pressing exhibits a markedly stiff response, as inferred from the consistently high Rockwell hardness grades across the bulk. Incorporation of the larger, more metallic Ta and Zr atoms expands the lattice but simultaneously introduces substantial lattice distortion, enhancing the resistance to elastic deformation without sacrificing stiffness. Moreover, the fine, homogenous grain structure generated during hot pressing suppresses grain‑boundary compliance, further raising the effective modulus. The combined effect of solid‑solution strengthening from the multi‑principal composition and the reduced compliance of the densely packed, defect‑free matrix explains why the alloy’s elastic modulus scales with the observed Rockwell hardness, reflecting a robust, bond‑dominated stiffness characteristic of refractory HEAs.

text: A dense, near‑equimolar MoReZrCrTi feedstock was fabricated by laser‑directed energy deposition using a 200 W fiber laser with a spot size of 0.3 mm and scan speeds ranging from 400 to 1200 mm s⁻¹, producing fully dense builds after post‑annealing at 1400 °C in argon. Compression tests were conducted at strain rates spanning 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻¹ s⁻¹, while tensile specimens were tested on a servo‑hydraulic test frame equipped with a 100 kN load cell. At lower strain rates, the alloy exhibited a modest yield plateau followed by strain hardening dominated by dislocation forest interactions within a fine equiaxed grain structure (~10 µm). As the strain rate increased, a pronounced rise in flow stress was observed, attributable to dynamic strain aging of Re and Zr solutes and the reduced time for recovery processes; this effect was most pronounced near 10⁻² s⁻¹. Grain boundary strengthening remained largely invariant, whereas the lattice distortion contributed to higher critical resolved shear stress at high rates, leading to an overall strain‑rate sensitivity coefficient of ~0.1. The microstructural analysis revealed no secondary phase formation, confirming that the observed rate dependence arises primarily from solid‑solution strengthening and solute drag effects.

The repeated reheating and cooling associated with layer‑by‑layer deposition refines the dendritic arm spacing, promoting a homogeneous distribution of solute and reducing segregation at grain boundaries. text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy HfVZrWCrNbMo, fabricated by vacuum induction melting and subsequent rapid cooling, exhibits a body‑centred cubic lattice with pronounced lattice distortion due to the disparate atomic sizes of its constituents. During exposure to humid environments, the high affinity of V and Nb for oxygen and hydrogen leads to the formation of interstitial oxides and hydrides at grain boundaries, promoting stress corrosion cracking. Micro‑diffraction studies reveal that hydrogen preferentially occupies octahedral sites, causing local lattice expansion and embrittlement, while simultaneously weakening the metallic bond network. The resulting softening is most pronounced along the <111> slip directions where dislocation mobility is reduced by the presence of Cr‑rich secondary phases. text: In HfTaVCr, the equiatomic mixture of refractory elements with significantly different atomic sizes and electronegativities drives the formation of a single body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution when processed by powder metallurgy followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). Rapid consolidation in SPS limits grain growth and preserves the high‑temperature BCC phase down to room temperature, preventing decomposition into intermetallics that typically occur during slow cooling. The lattice distortion introduced by the size mismatch among Hf, Ta, V, and Cr promotes solid solution strengthening, while the high melting points of the constituents suppress the nucleation of secondary phases. Thermodynamic calculations show that the Gibbs free energy of mixing for this composition remains negative across a broad temperature range, ensuring phase stability of the BCC solid solution. Consequently, the alloy retains a uniform microstructure with minimal porosity, providing a solid baseline for exploring mechanical performance such as yield strength and fracture toughness.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions

text: TiVNb, a refractory high‑entropy alloy fabricated by powder metallurgy and consolidated through spark‑plasma sintering, exemplifies the challenges of notch sensitivity in brittle body‑centered‑cubic (BCC) systems. The rapid densification inherent to SPS produces a relatively uniform microstructure, yet residual porosity and grain‑boundary carbides that form at the sintering temperature act as preferential sites for stress concentration when a sharp notch is introduced. Instrumented indentation mapping across the polished surface reveals that regions adjacent to the notch tip display a modest rise in measured hardness and a slight reduction in elastic modulus, reflecting localized constraint and the onset of microcracking. Because BCC refractory matrices lack extensive ductile slip systems, the elastic strain field cannot be readily relaxed, so the elevated hardness near the notch correlates with a lower fracture‑toughness response. Consequently, TiVNb’s fracture resistance is governed more by the distribution of these hardened zones and the ease with which cracks can link across grain boundaries than by bulk strength alone, underscoring the importance of controlling defect populations during SPS to mitigate notch‑driven brittleness.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: The hardness of suction‑cast refractory high‑entropy alloys is governed principally by the balance between lattice‑distortion strengthening of the solid‑solution matrix and the reinforcement provided by any secondary intermetallic phases that nucleate during rapid solidification. In ZrReTaTiV the constituent elements differ markedly in atomic size and electronegativity, producing a highly distorted body‑centered cubic matrix that already offers substantial resistance to dislocation glide; however, the relatively low melting points of Zr and Ti promote segregation of Ti‑rich and Zr‑rich clusters that can partially transform into brittle intermetallics, modestly increasing hardness but also introducing fracture‑prone interfaces. By contrast, WNbHfCrMoTiZr contains several very high‑melting refractory elements (W, Mo, Nb) whose mutual solubility suppresses extensive phase separation, yet the presence of Hf and Cr encourages the precipitation of fine Laves‑type compounds along grain boundaries. These finely dispersed secondary particles act as potent obstacles to dislocation motion, often yielding a harder overall response than the more uniformly distorted ZrReTaTiV matrix. Consequently, one would expect the WNbHfCrMoTiZr alloy to exhibit a higher hardness trend, principally because its microstructure combines strong solid‑solution strengthening with a higher volume fraction of finely distributed, hard intermetallic precipitates, whereas ZrReTaTiV relies chiefly on lattice distortion with fewer reinforcing phases.

subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy WHfZrTiVTa synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying and subsequently consolidated through hot pressing exhibits a distinctive recrystallization pathway governed by the interplay of severe lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion inherent to multi‑principal‑element systems. Initial milling produces a nanocrystalline assemblage with extensive defect networks that act as nucleation sites during the first stage of recovery, where sub‑grain rotation and annihilation of dislocations accelerate the formation of low‑energy grain boundaries. Upon heating above the characteristic recrystallization temperature, the high configurational entropy suppresses the growth of energetically favored orientations, leading to a prolonged incubation period before abnormal grain growth initiates. Grain coarsening follows a power‑law kinetics with an exponent lower than that of conventional refractory alloys, reflecting the combined effects of solute drag from W and Hf atoms and the persistent presence of Zr‑rich second‑phase particles that pin boundaries. The resulting microstructure comprises a bimodal grain size distribution, where fine grains retain elevated hardness and yield strength, while the coarser grains contribute to improved ductility and thermal stability.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: recrystallization behavior and grain growth kinetics

text: Powder‑metallurgy synthesis of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WVZr followed by spark‑plasma sintering yields a dense microstructure with sub‑10 µm grains and minimal porosity, prerequisites for stable high‑temperature surface performance. The alloy’s inherent lattice distortion and the sluggish diffusion of W, V, and Zr elements promote the formation of a continuous, thermally stable β‑phase matrix that resists grain growth up to 1200 °C. Surface oxidation studies indicate that a native Zr‑rich oxide film develops during initial exposure, providing a barrier against aggressive environments. To enhance coating effectiveness, a two‑layer strategy can be employed: first, a thin Cr‑containing interlayer deposited by electron‑beam evaporation improves adhesion and reduces thermal mismatch, while a subsequent topcoat of TiN or SiC deposited via chemical vapor deposition supplies a hard, thermally conductive layer that mitigates oxidation and spallation. This combinatorial approach capitalizes on the alloy’s intrinsic high‑temperature stability, resulting in improved oxidation resistance, reduced creep, and extended service life for coating or surface‑protected components.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: high-temperature coating or surface protection strategies

text: The vacuum‑induction‑melted CrWNbVReTiZr alloy exhibits pronounced lattice distortion owing to the wide span of atomic radii among its constituent elements, with Cr and V representing the smallest species and Zr and Re the largest. During solidification the rapid melt stirring inherent to induction heating promotes a homogeneous distribution of these size‑disparate atoms on a body‑centered cubic sublattice, yet the mismatch generates substantial local strain fields that impede dislocation glide and raise the critical resolved shear stress. First‑principles calculations suggest that the resulting elastic heterogeneity enhances the alloy’s resistance to plastic deformation without the need for secondary precipitates. Moreover, the retained high‑entropy mixing entropy stabilizes the distorted lattice against ordering transformations, preserving the solid‑solution strengthening effect across the entire temperature range examined. Consequently, the alloy’s microstructure is dominated by a single, heavily distorted phase in which atomic size mismatch is the primary contributor to its elevated strength and hardness.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: lattice distortion effects from atomic size mismatch

text: The two refractory high‑entropy alloys were synthesized by vacuum‑induction melting of elemental powders, followed by extrusion to generate a pronounced <001> texture that mimics the columnar grain structure typical of laser‑based additive manufacturing. In the HfVCrTaWReZr alloy, the large atomic size mismatch among Hf, W and Re creates substantial lattice distortion, which together with the presence of fine Cr‑rich carbides along grain boundaries enhances solid‑solution and precipitation strengthening preferentially along the loading direction parallel to the texture; consequently the longitudinal tensile response is expected to be markedly higher than the transverse one, with a pronounced strain‑rate sensitivity arising from the sluggish diffusion of the heavy elements. By contrast, VReTaZrTi exhibits a more balanced distribution of medium‑weight elements and a lower tendency to form continuous secondary phases, resulting in a comparatively weaker texture and a more isotropic grain‑boundary network; its tensile strength varies only modestly with orientation, while elongation remains relatively uniform. The contrasting anisotropy thus reflects the interplay of lattice distortion, carbide morphology, and texture intensity inherent to each composition.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: In laser‑directed energy deposition the rapid melt‑pool solidification inherent to TaReHfVMoNbW and HfCrVTiReTa generates markedly different solid‑solution strengthening contributions because of the contrasting atomic size mismatches and valence electron concentrations of the constituent elements. The Ta‑Re‑Hf‑V‑Mo‑Nb‑W alloy comprises seven refractory metals whose atomic radii span a relatively broad range, producing a high degree of lattice distortion that impedes dislocation motion and therefore elevates the yield strength relative to more modestly distorted systems. Moreover, the predominance of high‑valence‑electron‑density elements (Ta, Mo, W) enhances bond stiffness, further reinforcing the lattice. By contrast, HfCrVTiReTa replaces several of the heaviest, most mismatched atoms with lighter, less‑distorted species such as Cr, Ti, and V, which modestly reduces the overall lattice strain and yields a comparatively lower solid‑solution strengthening effect. Consequently, under otherwise identical processing conditions, the TaReHfVMoNbW composition is expected to exhibit a higher yield‑strength trend, while the HfCrVTiReTa alloy would tend toward a softer response, reflecting the balance between atomic size disparity, electron‑concentration effects, and the resulting resistance to dislocation glide.

text: Mechanical alloying of equiatomic NbMoWTaRe followed by hot pressing at elevated temperatures results in a single-phase body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid solution that remains stable up to the sintering temperature. The high atomic mismatch among Nb, Mo, W, Ta, and Re generates significant lattice distortion, suppressing the formation of intermetallic or orthorhombic secondary phases during consolidation. Rapid consolidation under pressure further limits grain growth, yielding a fine, equiaxed microstructure that enhances solid‑solution strengthening. Thermodynamic calculations predict a narrow miscibility gap on the NbMoW–Ta–Re system, corroborated by X‑ray diffraction which shows only the BCC Bragg peaks with minimal peak broadening, indicating a uniform distribution of constituent atoms. The absence of secondary phases reduces internal stresses and porosity, promoting mechanical integrity. Consequently, the alloy exhibits a stable BCC matrix with enhanced resistance to phase transformation, setting the stage for improved high‑temperature strength and fatigue resistance in subsequent mechanical testing.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy VZrCrTiNbMo, produced by arc‑melting and subsequent drop‑casting, adopts a single‑phase body‑centered cubic matrix whose extreme lattice distortion creates a dense network of high‑energy sites that readily attract interstitial hydrogen. Because each constituent element possesses a relatively low hydrogen solubility, dissolved H atoms tend to concentrate at grain boundaries, dislocation cores, and vacancy clusters, where they promote decohesion and facilitate crack initiation under tensile loading. The presence of Zr and Ti further enhances hydrogen trapping, while the strong metallic bonds among V, Nb, and Mo increase the overall resistance to diffusion, slowing the redistribution of H and allowing local accumulation. When the alloy is exposed to humid or reducing environments, surface oxide layers can crack, providing pathways for H ingress; the resulting hydrogen‑induced softening reduces the effective strain‑hardening capacity and accelerates intergranular fracture. Mitigating strategies therefore emphasize grain refinement, the introduction of stable carbide or nitride precipitates that serve as reversible hydrogen sinks, and post‑processing anneals that relieve residual stresses and reduce vacancy concentrations, all of which diminish the susceptibility of VZrCrTiNbMo to environmental embrittlement.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: environmental embrittlement and hydrogen effects
