text: Mechanical alloying of the refractory high‑entropy alloy CrTaTiRe was followed by hot‑pressing to produce dense bulk samples. Subsequent isothermal annealing at elevated temperatures induces pronounced microstructural evolution: the initially homogenous supersaturated solid solution decomposes into a dual‑phase microstructure comprising a primary BCC matrix and coherent Ti‑rich precipitates. Grain growth during annealing is limited by the high lattice distortion imposed by the large atomic size difference among Cr, Ta, Ti and Re, maintaining a fine‑grained matrix that promotes strength retention. The coherent Ti‑rich precipitates, spaced at sub‑micron intervals, act as effective Orowan obstacles, enhancing yield strength through precipitation strengthening while preserving ductility via load transfer between the matrix and precipitates. Moreover, homogenization reduces internal porosity and eliminates residual stress gradients introduced during hot‑pressing, thereby improving fracture toughness. Overall, controlled annealing tailors phase distribution, precipitate size, and grain structure to optimize the balance of strength, hardness, and toughness in CrTaTiRe.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: The Zr‑V‑W‑Re‑Hf‑Mo‑Ti refractory high‑entropy alloy fabricated by powder metallurgy and consolidated with spark‑plasma sintering exhibits a dense, fine‑grained body‑centered‑cubic matrix in which severe lattice distortion from the seven principal elements provides dominant solid‑solution strengthening. As temperature rises from ambient to the upper‑service range, the tensile strength and yield strength display a gradual decline, reflecting the thermally activated reduction of the Peierls barrier and the increased mobility of dislocations within the highly distorted lattice; however, the presence of nanoscale Hf‑rich precipitates, retained from the rapid sintering cycle, mitigates this softening by pinning dislocations and preserving a modest strength plateau at intermediate temperatures. Three‑point bend fracture‑toughness specimens tested according to ASTM E399/E1820 reveal a concurrent increase in crack‑tip opening displacement with temperature, indicating that the same mechanisms that lower the flow stress also promote greater plastic deformation ahead of a crack. Consequently, the alloy’s temperature‑dependent tensile and yield behavior correlates directly with the observed toughness evolution, underscoring the interplay between solid‑solution distortion, precipitate strengthening, and thermally activated slip in this refractory HEA.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: The NbTaZrTiMoWV alloy, with its five‑component refractory matrix, exhibits a pronounced temperature‑dependent strength retention that surpasses that of the binary CrHfTa system across the investigated range. The high configurational entropy and extensive lattice distortion produced by the equiatomic mixture of Nb, Ta, Zr, Ti, Mo, W and V generate strong solid‑solution strengthening, which is only modestly degraded as temperature rises; the presence of multiple high‑melting‑point constituents also delays diffusion‑controlled recovery, preserving dislocation forest density at elevated temperatures. In contrast, CrHfTa relies primarily on the strength contribution of Hf and the modest solid‑solution effect of Cr, so its yield strength declines more rapidly with heating, though the formation of fine Hf‑rich precipitates can modestly sustain strength at intermediate temperatures. Consequently, the NbTaZrTiMoWV alloy is expected to maintain a higher tensile and yield strength at both room temperature and elevated service temperatures, whereas CrHfTa will show a steeper drop in these properties as temperature increases.

subtopic: temperature dependence of tensile strength and yield strength

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy HfVReTiZrWTa, fabricated by mechanical alloying of elemental powders followed by spark‑plasma sintering, exhibits a pronounced work‑hardening response that can be inferred from its rising Rockwell hardness after successive tensile straining cycles. During deformation, the extreme lattice distortion created by the five‑element mix impedes dislocation glide, so each slip event leaves a dense forest of tangled dislocations. As strain accumulates, these dislocation networks interact with the fine‑grained (sub‑micron) matrix and with nanoscale secondary phases that often precipitate at grain boundaries during the rapid sintering cycle. The combined effect raises the resistance to further slip, which is reflected in the incremental increase of the Rockwell hardness measured on partially strained specimens. Moreover, the high melting points of Hf, V, Re, Ti, Zr, W, and Ta suppress dynamic recovery, ensuring that the stored dislocation density remains high throughout loading, thereby sustaining the steep work‑hardening slope characteristic of this refractory HEA.

text: The refractory alloy NbTaCrTiHfReV, produced by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot pressing, exhibits pronounced lattice distortion owing to the wide span of atomic radii among its constituent elements. The incorporation of relatively large Hf and Re atoms alongside smaller Cr and V creates a highly mismatched crystalline framework that deviates markedly from an ideal BCC lattice, generating a persistent strain field throughout the matrix. This strain impedes dislocation glide by raising the Peierls barrier and fostering a forest of short‑range ordered clusters that further lock slip systems. Consequently, the material displays a marked increase in strength and hardness relative to more size‑matched refractory systems, while retaining sufficient ductility because the distorted lattice also promotes multiple slip activation. Grain refinement achieved during milling amplifies these effects, as the distorted lattice interacts synergistically with grain‑boundary strengthening, leading to a robust combination of load‑bearing capability and thermal stability.

text: The vacuum‑induction‑melted VTaTiCrHf alloy displays a ductile response that is closely linked to its evolving microstructure; the as‑cast material consists of a single‑phase body‑centered cubic matrix whose lattice is heavily distorted by the size mismatch among V, Ta, Ti, Cr and Hf, providing substantial solid‑solution strengthening while preserving slip system activity. Grain refinement achieved during solidification promotes uniform deformation, yet the presence of residual Cr‑rich segregation bands at grain boundaries can act as preferential sites for strain localization, reducing the overall elongation. Minor amounts of Hf‑bearing precipitates nucleate during cooling and, if finely dispersed, they impede dislocation motion without catastrophically hindering glide, thereby maintaining reasonable ductility. Conversely, coarser Hf‑rich particles or extensive porosity introduced by incomplete melt homogenization serve to concentrate stress and trigger premature fracture. Optimizing cooling rates to suppress segregation and to achieve a narrow precipitate size distribution therefore enhances the alloy’s capacity to undergo large plastic strains before rupture.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: The strain‑rate sensitivity of strength in laser‑deposited refractory high‑entropy alloys was examined for two equiatomic compositions, VTiHfReTaZr and HfTaWZrMoNbV, each fabricated by directed‑energy deposition. The VTiHfReTaZr alloy, containing a larger fraction of low‑density transition metals (V, Ti) and the highly ductile element Re, exhibits a relatively compliant bcc lattice that accommodates dislocation motion more readily; consequently its flow stress rises modestly with increasing strain rate, reflecting a lower strain‑rate hardening exponent. In contrast, HfTaWZrMoNbV is enriched in heavy, high‑melting‑point elements (Ta, W, Mo, Nb) that generate pronounced lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening, producing a more pronounced rate‑dependent increase in flow stress. Additionally, the higher melting points of these constituents suppress dynamic recovery during rapid deformation, further amplifying strain‑rate sensitivity. Microstructural analysis reveals finer cellular substructures and reduced porosity in the HfTaWZrMoNbV deposits, which together rationalize its tendency toward greater strength augmentation under high‑rate loading relative to the VTiHfReTaZr system.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: strain rate sensitivity of strength properties

text: ReZrTaVCrWNb is a refractory high‑entropy alloy whose compressive response is strongly shaped by the interplay of lattice distortion, solid‑solution hardening, and the residual stress state imposed during suction casting in an argon atmosphere. The rapid solidification that characterises suction casting suppresses long‑range elemental segregation, yielding a nearly single‑phase body‑centered cubic matrix riddled with nanoscale chemical fluctuations; these fluctuations generate a high density of short‑range ordered clusters that impede dislocation glide more effectively under compression than under tension because the resolved shear stress aligns with the dominant slip systems. Moreover, the thermal gradient during solidification leaves a compressive residual stress field near the surface, which adds to the applied load and raises the apparent compressive yield point, whereas tensile loading must first overcome the opposing tensile residual stress, producing a lower apparent tensile yield. Grain refinement, often achieved by post‑cast cold working, further accentuates this asymmetry, as finer grains promote a Hall‑Petch‑type increase in compressive strength while having a less pronounced effect on tensile yield due to the already limited slip activity in the highly distorted lattice.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy WMoVZrTaTiRe, produced by vacuum arc melting and subsequent drop‑casting, exhibits a markedly different high‑temperature response than conventional Ni‑based superalloys. Its constituent refractory elements generate a severely distorted BCC lattice, which imparts intrinsic solid‑solution strengthening that persists to temperatures where γ′‑strengthened Ni alloys begin to soften. In addition, the rapid solidification inherent to drop‑casting suppresses the formation of coarse intermetallic networks, yielding a fine, cellular substructure that further raises the yield strength and creep resistance at elevated temperatures. Unlike Ni‑based superalloys, whose performance relies on ordered precipitates that can coarsen under thermal exposure, the WMoVZrTaTiRe matrix retains its strength through lattice distortion and limited precipitation of stable Zr‑rich compounds. Consequently, the alloy maintains a higher modulus and lower creep strain rate under prolonged service, while its oxidation resistance benefits from the protective Zr‑O surface layer that forms in air, offering a promising alternative for extreme‑temperature turbine and aerospace applications.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: comparison with conventional Ni-based superalloys in high-temperature contexts

text: The tensile and yield responses of MoNbHfReWTi and NbTaReCrTi evolve quite differently with temperature because the two chemistries impose distinct lattice‑distortion and solid‑solution strengthening fields while their powder‑metallurgy routes generate comparable grain sizes and residual porosity. In MoNbHfReWTi, the presence of large‑atomic‑radius Hf and the high‑Z element Re creates an especially severe mismatch among the five principal elements, which sustains a high density of short‑range order clusters that impede dislocation motion even as thermal activation rises; consequently the alloy retains a relatively gentle decline in both tensile and yield strength up to intermediate temperatures. By contrast, NbTaReCrTi relies on a more moderate size disparity and includes Cr, which tends to form a dispersed BCC‑type intermetallic network that is effective at low temperatures but softens more rapidly when thermal vibration assists dislocation climb around the weaker precipitates. As a result, NbTaReCrTi typically exhibits a steeper loss of strength with heating, placing MoNbHfReWTi on the higher‑strength side over a broad temperature range, while both alloys converge toward similar values only at very high temperatures where lattice‑distortion effects are largely overcome by thermal softening.

text: Laser additive manufacturing of the refractory high‑entropy alloy CrNbTaReTi by directed energy deposition produced a microstructure characterized by columnar grains elongated along the build direction and a pronounced texture dominated by the <001> axis. Grain refinement was observed when the laser power was increased and the scanning speed decreased, leading to a denser microstructure with fewer melt‑pool defects. Solid‑solution strengthening arises from the substantial lattice distortion induced by the five principal elements, particularly the large atomic radius mismatch between Cr and Re relative to the other constituents. As grain size is reduced, the yield strength of the alloy increases in accordance with the Hall‑Petch relationship, while the ultimate tensile strength shows only a modest rise because the alloy retains a high degree of intrinsic strength from the multicomponent solid solution. Thus, processing parameters that promote finer grains without compromising chemical homogeneity are critical for maximizing tensile performance in CrNbTaReTi.

text: The mechanically alloyed‑and‑hot‑pressed MoTiCrTa system displays a markedly higher Young’s modulus than the more compositionally complex HfTaCrNbTiV alloy, a consequence of its predominance of early‑transition metals with strong d‑orbital overlap and relatively short, covalent‑metallic bonds. Molybdenum and titanium contribute high intrinsic stiffness through extensive 4d–5d electron delocalization, while chromium and tantalum reinforce the lattice by augmenting the valence electron concentration, which raises the bulk modulus and, consequently, the elastic response. In contrast, the inclusion of hafnium, niobium and vanadium introduces larger atomic radii and a greater degree of lattice distortion, softening the average bond stiffness; the resulting increased lattice parameter and more pronounced solid‑solution strain reduce the overall Young’s modulus despite the presence of several high‑modulus constituents. Thus, the MoTiCrTa alloy is expected to trend toward a stiffer elastic behavior, whereas the HfTaCrNbTiV composition should exhibit a comparatively lower modulus owing to its expanded, more distorted crystal lattice.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy CrMoRe synthesized by powder metallurgy and consolidated through spark‑plasma sintering exhibits a pronounced Hall‑Petch response, wherein progressively refined grains produce concurrent increases in both yield strength and Vickers hardness. Microstructural analysis reveals that sub‑micron grains, stabilized by the high lattice distortion inherent to the Cr‑Mo‑Re system, impede dislocation glide more effectively than coarse‑grained counterparts, generating a steep rise in flow stress that is reflected in the hardness measurements. Cyclic fatigue experiments demonstrate that specimens with finer microstructures sustain a markedly longer fatigue life at comparable stress amplitudes, a benefit attributed to the reduced slip‑band spacing and the higher resistance to crack initiation afforded by the dense grain boundary network. Conversely, coarser grains promote early crack nucleation and faster propagation, shortening the endurance limit despite comparable nominal compositions. These observations underscore grain‑size engineering as a pivotal lever for simultaneously optimizing strength, hardness, and fatigue durability in CrMoRe alloys.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: The tensile response of laser‑deposited TaReVNbW and CrZrTiVHfTa was examined to elucidate their contrasting work‑hardening trajectories, revealing that the former alloy consistently exhibits a steeper hardening rate than the latter. In TaReVNbW, the high concentration of refractory transition metals produces pronounced lattice distortion and a dense forest of dislocations that are impeded by strong solid‑solution strengthening and a fine dispersion of BCC‑type sub‑grains generated during rapid solidification; these obstacles promote extensive dislocation multiplication and dynamic recovery is limited, yielding a sustained increase in flow stress with strain. Conversely, CrZrTiVHfTa contains a broader mix of high‑Zr and Hf atoms that favor the formation of nanoscale Laves‑phase precipitates and modestly larger grain sizes, which act as early pinning sites but also facilitate cross‑slip and limited dynamic recrystallization, thereby tempering the work‑hardening slope. The combined effect of greater lattice strain energy and reduced recovery in TaReVNbW rationalizes its higher work‑hardening propensity relative to CrZrTiVHfTa.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: work hardening behavior during tensile deformation

text: The tensile response of laser‑deposited HfNbCrZrVMoW, recorded with an extensometer, reveals a clear Hall‑Petch correlation: specimens exhibiting finer columnar grains along the build direction consistently display elevated flow stress and higher indentation hardness. Rapid solidification inherent to directed‑energy deposition produces a steep thermal gradient, refining the dendritic arms and suppressing grain coarsening; the resulting sub‑micron cellular substructures impede dislocation glide more effectively than the coarser equiaxed grains found in slower‑cooled regions. Consequently, the finer‑grained zones sustain larger load increments before necking, and their extensometer curves show a steeper slope in the elastic‑plastic transition, reflecting increased yield resistance. In contrast, regions with larger grains show a more gradual strain accumulation and reduced hardness, indicating that grain‑boundary strengthening dominates over solid‑solution effects in this refractory HEA. The observed trend underscores the importance of controlling cooling rates during deposition to tailor grain size and, thereby, optimize strength and hardness.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: The MoTaTiCrNbZrV refractory high‑entropy alloy was synthesized by high‑energy ball milling under argon for several hours until a homogeneous fine‑grained powder was obtained, after which the mixture was consolidated by hot pressing at temperatures exceeding the melting points of the constituent binaries but below the onset of excessive grain growth. Specimens machined from the dense billets were notched with a razor‑cut V‑groove of controlled radius and subsequently polished to a mirror finish to eliminate surface defects. Fracture tests revealed a pronounced notch sensitivity: the measured fracture toughness dropped sharply as the notch tip radius decreased, reflecting the limited plastic zone that can develop in the predominantly BCC matrix. Scanning electron microscopy of the fracture surfaces showed a largely transgranular cleavage pattern with occasional intergranular facets where residual porosity or Cr‑rich secondary phases acted as crack initiators. The observations underscore that, in this alloy, lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening raise the theoretical strength but also constrain ductile deformation, so that even modest stress concentrations at sharp notches dramatically reduce the apparent fracture resistance.

text: The refractory alloy CrReMoHf, fabricated by consolidating elemental powders through spark‑plasma sintering, exemplifies how severe lattice distortion can dominate its mechanical response. Because chromium, rhenium, molybdenum and hafnium differ markedly in atomic radius, the random occupation of a simple body‑centered cubic or hexagonal lattice creates a highly irregular strain field around each substitutional site. This strain field resists dislocation motion by forcing the glide plane to accommodate fluctuating interatomic distances, a mechanism that is amplified when the powder particles are fully densified under the rapid heating and pressure of SPS, preserving the high‑entropy solid solution. The resulting short‑range order further distorts the crystal potential, raising the effective Peierls barrier and promoting work hardening. Grain refinement that typically accompanies SPS also synergizes with distortion‑based strengthening, because smaller grains increase the density of grain‑boundary obstacles while the lattice itself remains intrinsically resistant to slip. Consequently, CrReMoHf displays a pronounced combination of high yield strength and hardness that is rooted primarily in the atomic‑size mismatch‑driven distortion of its crystal lattice.

subtopic: lattice distortion effects from atomic size mismatch

text: The V‑Cr‑Zr alloy series was prepared by arc‑melting stoichiometric mixtures of high‑purity V, Cr, and Zr under a Ti‑getter atmosphere, each button being flipped and remelted three times to ensure homogeneity before being drop‑cast onto a copper chill plate. Optical microscopy revealed a dendritic‑eutectic microstructure in which the Zr‑rich interdendritic regions contained a fine lamellar mixture of bcc solid solution and a Zr‑bearing intermetallic that became progressively more continuous as the Zr fraction increased. Vickers indentation showed that alloys with modest Zr content exhibited the highest hardness, a consequence of the combined effects of solid‑solution strengthening from V and Cr and the dispersion of nanoscale intermetallic particles that impede dislocation motion. When Zr exceeded a critical level, the intermetallic network coalesced into a continuous brittle phase, reducing the overall hardness despite the larger lattice distortion, because the softer bcc matrix was effectively depleted. Heat‑treated specimens in which the intermetallic was partially dissolved displayed a modest recovery of hardness, underscoring the dominant role of secondary‑phase morphology over simple compositional ratios.

text: The refractory alloy WVHfNb, assembled by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot‑press sintering, forms a single‑phase body‑centered‑cubic matrix whose extreme lattice distortion and high melting constituents confer remarkable thermal stability for coating applications. During mechanical alloying, repeated fracture‑weld cycles produce nanometer‑scale compositional mixing, while the subsequent hot‑press step promotes diffusion‑driven homogenization without excessive grain growth, preserving a fine grain structure that impedes high‑temperature diffusion creep. The substantial mismatch in atomic size among W, V, Hf, and Nb generates strong solid‑solution strengthening, which together with the high intrinsic oxidation resistance of Hf and the refractory nature of W and Nb, yields a surface layer that remains coherent under prolonged exposure to oxidizing atmospheres. Moreover, the low porosity achieved by hot pressing limits pathways for oxygen ingress, while residual compressive residual stresses from rapid densification further suppress spallation. Consequently, WVHfNb coatings can sustain protective performance at temperatures where conventional superalloys begin to soften, making the alloy especially suitable for turbine blade or furnace liner protection.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy TaMoReZrV fabricated by directed‑energy deposition exhibits a pronounced temperature dependence of its tensile and yield strengths, which can be rationalized through the microstructural evolution captured during compact‑tension fracture‑toughness testing. At cryogenic temperatures the alloy retains a single‑phase body‑centered cubic matrix with extreme lattice distortion, and the resulting solid‑solution strengthening, coupled with limited dislocation mobility, yields a markedly high tensile strength and a steep yield‑point offset. As temperature rises toward the intermediate regime, thermally activated glide and cross‑slip increase, reducing the yield stress while the tensile strength declines more gradually owing to the retention of a high density of nanoscale sub‑grains formed during rapid solidification. Near the onset of recrystallization, partial precipitation of Zr‑rich carbides provides secondary strengthening, moderating the loss of strength and sustaining modest fracture toughness. At elevated temperatures the combined effects of lattice softening, precipitate coarsening, and enhanced diffusion lead to a further reduction in both tensile and yield strengths, while the compact‑tension data reveal a concomitant transition from ductile‑cleavage mixed fracture to predominantly ductile tearing.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrCrReNb was produced by suction casting into a chilled copper mold under a high‑purity argon atmosphere, yielding a near‑fully dense, single‑phase body‑centered cubic matrix with modest compositional segregation at interdendritic regions. Subsequent exposure to humid environments revealed pronounced embrittlement that intensified with increasing hydrogen uptake, as hydrogen preferentially occupied interstitial sites near Cr‑rich clusters and promoted lattice dilation that amplified the already high atomic misfit inherent to the multi‑principal composition. In situ charging experiments showed that trapped hydrogen reduced the cohesive strength of Zr‑Cr bonds, facilitating decohesion along grain boundaries that had been weakened by residual porosity from the casting process. Microstructural analysis indicated that the presence of nano‑scale Re‑rich precipitates acted as hydrogen traps, partially mitigating crack propagation but also serving as sites for hydrogen‑induced decohesion under tensile loading. Overall, the study underscores the critical role of hydrogen‑induced lattice distortion and grain‑boundary chemistry in governing the environmental susceptibility of ZrCrReNb, offering guidance for alloy design and processing routes that minimize hydrogen ingress.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: environmental embrittlement and hydrogen effects

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy HfCrTiVNbRe was fabricated by directed‑energy deposition using a fiber laser operating at a power sufficient to fully melt the powder feedstock while maintaining a stable keyhole mode; the powder was delivered through a coaxial nozzle at a rate that produced a fully dense clad with a shallow melt pool geometry. After deposition, the as‑built surfaces displayed a characteristic dendritic–cellular substructure, with Cr‑rich interdendritic filaments and Nb‑enriched cores, and a modest level of surface roughness that was subsequently reduced by a light mechanical polishing step. To endow the component with high‑temperature oxidation resistance, a thin Al‑containing slurry was sprayed onto the alloy and subsequently laser‑remelted in situ, forming a continuous Al‑rich oxide scale that adhered to the underlying HfCrTiVNbRe matrix. Complementary experiments employed a vapor‑phase Y₂O₃ coating applied by pulsed laser deposition, which generated a nanocrystalline yttria layer that acted as a diffusion barrier at temperatures where the base alloy begins to oxidize. Cross‑sectional microscopy revealed that both coating routes produced a well‑bonded interface with minimal delamination after cyclic heating to several hundred degrees Celsius, and energy‑dispersive spectroscopy confirmed the retention of the original alloy composition beneath the protective layers.

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbVWMoRe under an inert argon atmosphere produced dense, columnar‑grained microstructures with minor oxide inclusions. Vickers microhardness measurements performed at 4.9 N loading over twenty sites revealed a consistent hardness band of 2600–2800 HV, with local peaks approaching 2900 HV in regions adjacent to coarse intergranular Mo‑rich precipitates. The uniform hardness distribution implies effective solid‑solution strengthening from the large lattice distortion inherent to the Nb/V/W/Mo/Re system, while the modest hardness variation indicates limited secondary‑phase contribution. Notch‑sensitive fracture tests on miniature V‑shaped specimens showed a pronounced drop in fracture toughness relative to polished samples, suggesting that the high hardness, low fracture strain, and the predominance of BCC bonding render the alloy particularly susceptible to crack initiation at geometric stress concentrators. The correlation between localized hardness elevations and reduced energy absorption before catastrophic failure underscores the importance of minimizing micro‑defects and optimizing grain size to mitigate notch sensitivity in this brittle HEA.

subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: The refractory system V‑Ti‑Cr illustrates how severe plastic deformation combined with rapid consolidation can drive a near‑equiatomic mixture toward a single‑phase body‑centered‑cubic (BCC) solid solution, despite the considerable differences in atomic radius among the three constituents. During mechanical alloying, repeated fracture and cold welding generate nanometer‑scale compositional lamellae that promote extensive lattice distortion; the high density of crystal defects supplies diffusion pathways that accelerate interdiffusion when the powder is subsequently hot‑pressed at temperatures well below the melting points of the individual elements. Under these conditions the Gibbs free energy of a disordered BCC lattice is reduced relative to any ordered intermetallic configuration, because the configurational entropy of mixing outweighs the enthalpic penalty associated with size mismatch. The resulting BCC phase retains a homogeneous distribution of V, Ti, and Cr atoms, with only trace amounts of residual oxides or porosity, and exhibits a stable crystal structure over a broad temperature range, providing a robust baseline for subsequent alloying or thermomechanical treatments.

text: In the powder‑metallurgical route to HfNbTa, the initial mixing of elemental powders followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) tends to produce a dense body with residual porosity that is highly non‑uniform. Nanoindentation mapping reveals that regions containing finer, equiaxed grains exhibit higher local hardness and elastic modulus relative to coarse, lamellar zones, indicating effective solid‑solution strengthening from lattice distortion by the three high‑entropy elements. However, pores that remain within the coarse‑grained matrix act as stress concentrators, reducing the energy required for crack initiation and propagation. Consequently, fracture toughness measured by micro‑cantilever bending is noticeably lower in specimens with larger interconnected pores, while fatigue crack growth rates increase sharply at stress amplitudes just below the yield point. The local mechanical property contrast captured by the hardness and modulus maps thus directly correlates with the observed degradation in fatigue life: regions of reduced modulus and hardness, often adjacent to pores or secondary TiO₂‑rich inclusions, serve as preferential initiation sites for sub‑surface fatigue cracks.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloys TaReNbZrW and MoTiWVCrReHf were synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot pressing under comparable loads, yet the resulting microstructures differed markedly in residual porosity and defect populations. In TaReNbZrW, the relatively low melting points of Ta and Zr promote grain growth during consolidation, which, coupled with incomplete densification, yields a network of sub‑micron pores that act as crack nucleation sites and blunt crack propagation, thereby reducing fracture toughness and accelerating fatigue crack initiation under cyclic loading. Conversely, MoTiWVCrReHf benefits from the higher melting temperatures of Mo, W, and Hf, which suppress excessive grain coarsening and facilitate a more uniform densification; the limited porosity is confined to isolated, nanometer‑scale voids that minimally perturb the crack tip stress field, resulting in a higher effective fracture toughness and a slower fatigue crack growth rate. Accordingly, the Mo‑based HEA is expected to exhibit a superior toughness‑fatigue trade‑off, whereas the Ta‑based alloy would trend lower in both metrics owing to its more pervasive processing defects.

text: The refractory alloy VReTi, produced by vacuum‑induction melting and subsequently homogenized, adopts a body‑centered‑cubic matrix that is intrinsically brittle because the constituent transition metals generate a high degree of lattice distortion and limited slip systems at ambient temperature. In such BCC‑dominated systems, the presence of a sharp notch concentrates elastic strain and promotes crack initiation at the tip, a phenomenon termed notch sensitivity. The degree of sensitivity is amplified when the microstructure contains coarse, columnar grains that align with the loading direction, because grain‑boundary facets provide preferential pathways for cleavage. Conversely, refining the grain size or introducing a modest dispersion of nanoscale Re‑rich precipitates can blunt the stress concentration, allowing limited plastic deformation ahead of the crack tip and thereby raising the apparent fracture toughness. Porosity or residual melt‑pool voids further exacerbate notch sensitivity, as they act as auxiliary stress raisers that lower the energy required for crack propagation. Understanding how grain morphology, secondary phase distribution, and residual defects interact with the stress field at a notch is therefore essential for predicting and improving the fracture‑toughness performance of VReTi.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: TiVCrTa fabricated by directed‑energy deposition exhibits a thermodynamically driven single‑phase BCC solid solution despite the pronounced chemical disparity among its constituent refractory elements. Calculations of the configurational entropy reveal a value that approaches the ideal high‑entropy limit, thereby offsetting the mildly positive mixing enthalpies associated with Ti–Cr and Cr–Ta pair interactions and stabilizing the disordered matrix at the rapid cooling rates inherent to laser deposition. The valence‑electron‑concentration of the alloy resides near the critical range that favors BCC over HCP structures, reinforcing the formation of a lattice‑distorted framework in which atomic size mismatch contributes additional strain energy. First‑principles assessments indicate that the combined effect of elevated entropy, moderate enthalpic penalties, and optimal VEC suppresses the nucleation of intermetallic compounds, promoting compositional homogeneity across the deposited tracks. This thermodynamic balance underlies the observed microstructural uniformity and provides a pathway for tailoring other refractory HEAs through controlled VEC and mixing enthalpy design.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: thermodynamic considerations (mixing enthalpy, valence electron concentration)

text: The arc‑melted, drop‑cast specimens of the refractory high‑entropy alloys ReTaWTiHfNb and TaWReNbZrCrMo exhibit markedly different grain morphologies that govern their mechanical response. In the ReTaWTiHfNb alloy, rapid solidification during drop casting yields a fine equiaxed microstructure with an average grain size in the sub‑10 µm range, whereas the TaWReNbZrCrMo alloy retains a coarser grain network (≈ 30–40 µm) due to a slower cooling rate and the presence of secondary intermetallic precipitates that impede grain boundary migration. According to Hall‑Petch behavior, the smaller grains in ReTaWTiHfNb provide a higher grain‑boundary density, leading to enhanced barrier to dislocation motion and therefore a higher yield strength and hardness relative to TaWReNbZrCrMo. Additionally, the more uniform solute distribution in ReTaWTiHfNb reduces local lattice distortion, further reinforcing its strength. Conversely, the larger grains and associated intermetallic networks in TaWReNbZrCrMo facilitate easier dislocation glide, resulting in lower strength and hardness while potentially improving ductility.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: the relationship between grain size and both strength and hardness (Hall-Petch-type reasoning)

text: The present work evaluates notch sensitivity and its impact on fracture toughness for two refractory high‑entropy alloys synthesized by mechanical alloying and consolidated by hot pressing: the binary‑derived MoZrCrTi system and the multicomponent TiVReHfTaCrNb composition. Both alloys adopt a body‑centered cubic lattice, yet the former exhibits a comparatively simpler elemental mix and a higher proportion of low‑melt‑point Zr, which promotes lattice distortion but also encourages the formation of brittle intermetallic clusters at grain boundaries. In contrast, the TiVReHfTaCrNb alloy contains a broader spectrum of transition‑metal refractory elements that generate pronounced solid‑solution strengthening and suppress extensive intermetallic precipitation, yielding a more uniform grain‑boundary chemistry. Consequently, the TiVReHfTaCrNb alloy displays reduced notch sensitivity, as crack tip plasticity is modestly enhanced by its finer, equiaxed grain structure and lower residual porosity, leading to a higher effective fracture‑toughness trend. The MoZrCrTi alloy, with coarser grains and a propensity for brittle phase segregation, is expected to be more notch‑sensitive and to exhibit lower fracture toughness under comparable loading conditions.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: Powder‑metallurgy fabrication followed by spark‑plasma sintering produces dense WCrHf and WHfTaTiCrMo specimens in which the alloying elements occupy a body‑centered cubic lattice with substantial lattice distortion. In WCrHf, the high concentration of the transition metal W and the relatively low amount of the late transition metal Hf lead to strong solid‑solution hardening but also promote the formation of coarse Cr‑rich secondary phases at high sintering temperatures, which tend to act as stress concentrators. These precipitates elevate the ultimate tensile and yield strengths, yet their coarse size and reduced interconnectivity limit dislocation mobility, causing the alloy to exhibit reduced strain‑to‑fracture compared to its counterpart. Conversely, the addition of Ta and Ti in WHfTaTiCrMo increases lattice distortion and supplies fine, coherently dispersed second‑phase particles that impede dislocation slip more uniformly. This results in a slightly lower peak strength than WCrHf but a more favorable ductility–strength balance, as the finer dispersion allows greater uniform plastic deformation before fracture.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)

text: The TaMoHf refractory high‑entropy alloy produced by directed‑energy deposition exhibits a consistently high elastic response that mirrors the strong metallic‑covalent bonding inherent to the transition‑metal matrix; the presence of Hf introduces a modest lattice expansion while preserving the high electron density contributed by Ta and Mo, thereby reinforcing the overall bond stiffness. Microhardness surveys performed with Vickers indents at numerous locations reveal a narrow scatter in hardness, indicating a uniform microstructure dominated by a single‑phase BCC solid solution with limited elemental segregation. This homogeneity translates into a relatively invariant Young’s modulus across the scanned area, as the elastic modulus is chiefly governed by the average bond strength rather than localized hardening features. Slight variations in indentation depth correlate with minor grain‑size fluctuations, yet the dominant contribution to the elastic modulus remains the intrinsic bonding character of the Ta‑Mo‑Hf system, underscoring its suitability for load‑bearing applications where stiffness consistency is paramount.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: In the WTiReTaZrCrHf refractory high‑entropy alloy synthesized through mechanical alloying and subsequent hot‑pressing, the observed hardness enhancement correlates strongly with the emergence and distribution of secondary phases rather than the homogeneous solid‑solution matrix alone. Fine, dispersed precipitates of Ti‑rich and Zr‑rich intermetallics form during the high‑temperature consolidation step, acting as obstacles to dislocation motion and thereby providing solid‑solution and precipitation strengthening in tandem. As the volume fraction of these coherent precipitates increases, grain boundary pinning becomes more pronounced, which further inhibits grain growth during the sintering cycle and maintains a fine‑grained microstructure that is inherently harder. Conversely, a coarsening of the precipitates or the formation of large, brittle intermetallic networks reduces the overall hardness by introducing localized weak zones where dislocations can bypass obstacles more readily. Thus, controlled precipitation of nanoscale secondary phases during hot‑pressing is the principal driver of the enhanced hardness in this system.

subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: The tensile response of refractory high‑entropy alloys fabricated by powder metallurgy and consolidated through spark‑plasma sintering is strongly modulated by crystallographic texture imparted during additive‑manufacturing or directional solidification, and the two compositions examined, WReHfNbV and TaReZrNbWCrV, illustrate contrasting anisotropic trends. In WReHfNbV, the dominant body‑centered cubic matrix is enriched with high‑Zr‑group elements that generate pronounced lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening, yet the relatively low stacking‑fault energy promotes the development of strong <100> fiber texture along the build direction; this alignment yields higher longitudinal yield and ultimate stresses but reduces ductility transverse to the loading axis. By contrast, TaReZrNbWCrV contains a more balanced mixture of transition‑metal and refractory‑metal constituents, fostering a dual‑phase microstructure with fine B2‑type precipitates that tend to randomize grain orientations during SPS; the resulting weaker texture diminishes longitudinal‑direction strengthening while preserving more isotropic elongation and fracture resistance. Consequently, WReHfNbV is expected to exhibit the higher peak tensile strength in the build direction, whereas TaReZrNbWCrV should display a lower anisotropy ratio and comparatively superior transverse ductility.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: anisotropy of tensile properties in additively manufactured or textured samples

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaVMoNbTiHf was carried out in an argon‑purged chamber to suppress oxidation; the melt, held above 2600 °C, was rapidly injected into a pre‑cooled copper mold, resulting in a fully dense ingot with a columnar grain structure oriented along the casting direction. After homogenization annealing at 1900 °C, specimens were machined into compact‑tension geometry for fracture toughness evaluation. During load‑controlled testing, the initial crack opening exhibited a linear elastic response, from which Young’s modulus was extracted by fitting the elastic portion of the load‑displacement curve. The measured modulus increased progressively with the proportion of transition metals possessing high valence electron density, indicating that the predominant covalent‑metallic bonding in the Ta–Nb–V–Mo–Ti–Hf lattice stiffens the crystal framework. Conversely, the presence of Ti, with its larger atomic radius, introduced local lattice distortions that slightly reduced the overall modulus relative to a pure Ta‑based alloy. The observed modulus trend aligns with the theoretical prediction that stronger bonding character, driven by high electronegativity contrast and dense d‑orbital overlap, enhances lattice stiffness, thereby influencing the initiation and propagation of cracks during compact‑tension testing.

subtopic: elastic (Young's) modulus trends and their relation to bonding character and composition

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy ReMoWVNbCrTa was synthesized by vacuum‑induction melting and subsequently subjected to conventional tensile testing in accordance with ASTM E8, revealing a pronounced strength‑ductility interplay characteristic of multicomponent BCC systems. Microstructural examination showed a predominance of a single‑phase BCC solid solution with modest lattice distortion, while residual Cr‑rich segregations acted as hard, brittle obstacles that elevated yield and ultimate tensile strengths but simultaneously promoted early strain localisation. Specimens with finer grain size and reduced porosity displayed higher flow stress, yet their elongation to fracture diminished as grain‑boundary sliding became constrained by the stiff matrix. Conversely, samples annealed to coarsen grains and dissolve minor Cr‑rich precipitates exhibited modest reductions in strength but recovered appreciable ductility, as evidenced by more uniform necking and delayed onset of microcrack nucleation. These observations underscore that optimizing ReMoWVNbCrTa for structural applications requires balancing solid‑solution strengthening against the detrimental effect of brittle second phases on tensile ductility.

subtopic: ductility-strength trade-offs (how gains in strength typically come at the cost of elongation)

text: The TiZrReHf refractory high‑entropy alloy, synthesized by vacuum arc melting and subsequently solidified through drop casting, exhibits a pronounced dependence of hardness on the relative proportion of each constituent element and the accompanying evolution of secondary phase fractions. Increasing the Re content tends to promote the formation of a Re‑rich intermetallic lamellae that decorates the primary body‑centered cubic matrix, and these hard precipitates act as potent barriers to dislocation glide, thereby elevating the bulk hardness. Conversely, augmenting Ti or Zr at the expense of Hf suppresses the nucleation of the Re‑rich phase, leading to a more homogeneous solid‑solution microstructure where lattice distortion dominates; the resulting hardness is modestly lower but still exceeds that of the constituent pure metals. Grain refinement induced by the rapid solidification inherent to drop casting further accentuates hardness across all compositions, especially when the secondary phase distribution is finely spaced rather than coarsened, underscoring the synergistic role of compositional tuning and microstructural control.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: qualitative hardness trends across compositions and their relation to secondary phase content

text: Arc melting of the equiatomic mixtures ZrReHfWTi and NbCrTaTiHf was followed by rapid drop casting to produce cast ingots with minimal cooling gradients. Post‑solidification, specimens were machined into notched dog‑bone coupons, with notch radii of 0.5 mm, and subjected to monotonic tensile loading to failure. The BCC framework of both alloys, coupled with high lattice distortion, promotes a high density of twin boundaries that act as barriers to crack propagation. However, the ZrReHfWTi composition incorporates Zr and Ti, which tend to stabilize a more ductile microstructure and increase the propensity for microcrack deflection, thereby reducing notch sensitivity and yielding comparatively higher fracture toughness. In contrast, NbCrTaTiHf contains a higher fraction of Cr and Nb, elements that favor the formation of fine, coherent precipitates that can act as crack initiators, raising notch sensitivity and diminishing fracture toughness. Consequently, the ZrReHfWTi alloy is expected to exhibit a lower notch effect and better fracture resistance than NbCrTaTiHf.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting

text: Powder‑metallurgy routes were employed to fabricate VWHfTiCrMoTa and TiVHfZrMo, each consolidated by spark plasma sintering at 1800 °C under 60 MPa for 5 min, yielding near‑full density compacts with fine equiaxed grains. Compression tests on cylindrical specimens revealed that VWHfTiCrMoTa exhibited a pronounced asymmetry relative to its tensile counterpart: the compressive yield stress was markedly higher, reflecting the enhanced resistance of the bcc lattice to densification and the stabilizing influence of the high‑entropy solid solution formed by V, W, Hf, Ti, Cr, Mo, and Ta. In contrast, TiVHfZrMo displayed a smaller yield asymmetry, with compressive yield stress only modestly exceeding its tensile yield. This difference is attributed to the partial substitution of Zr, which promotes the formation of nanoscale intergranular TiH phases, softening the compressive response. Consequently, VWHfTiCrMoTa is expected to trend higher in compressive yield strength due to its more coherent solid solution and reduced susceptibility to intergranular weakening.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: TiVTa alloys produced by vacuum arc melting and subsequent drop‑casting exhibit a robust body‑centered cubic (BCC) solid‑solution matrix that persists across a wide range of cooling rates, reflecting the high configurational entropy inherent to refractory systems. Energy‑dispersive spectroscopy confirms near‑equiatomic distribution of Ti, V, and Ta, while X‑ray diffraction reveals a single BCC phase with lattice parameters intermediate between those of the constituent elements, indicative of substantial lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening. Thermodynamic calculations suggest that the negative mixing enthalpy among Ti, V, and Ta suppresses intermetallic precipitation, while the elevated melting points of the components favor retention of the high‑temperature BCC structure upon solidification. Microstructural inspection shows a fine, dendritic‑cellular morphology with minimal segregation, further reinforcing phase stability. The combined effect of high entropy, moderate atomic size mismatch, and strong metallic bonding underlies the alloy’s resistance to phase separation, positioning TiVTa as a promising candidate for high‑temperature structural applications.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: phase stability and the formation of BCC solid solutions

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy CrTaTiRe was synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot pressing, producing a dense polycrystalline body with a pronounced supersaturated solid solution and residual strain fields. Subsequent annealing at intermediate temperatures promotes diffusion‑driven homogenization, reducing lattice distortion and dissolving mechanically induced nanoclusters while preserving the body‑centered cubic matrix. Grain growth proceeds from the fine sub‑micron regime toward larger equiaxed grains, which diminishes the density of high‑angle grain boundaries and alters the dislocation network. The reduction of internal stresses and the coarsening of secondary precipitates, chiefly Ti‑rich and Re‑enriched phases, lead to a more uniform compositional distribution and a decrease in local compositional segregation. Overall, the heat‑treatment pathway transforms the as‑pressed microstructure from a highly defect‑rich, heterogeneous state to a thermodynamically equilibrated configuration, establishing a foundation for systematic tuning of mechanical response through controlled grain size and precipitate morphology.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: the effect of annealing or homogenization heat treatment on microstructure

text: The comparative assessment of elongation at fracture for the spark‑plasma‑sintered refractory systems WTaVCr and HfReVTiCr reveals distinct microstructural controls on ductility. In the W‑rich alloy, the dominant body‑centered cubic matrix retains a relatively low lattice‑distortion energy because W, Ta, V, and Cr share similar atomic radii and valence electron concentrations; this facilitates the formation of a fine, equiaxed grain structure during rapid consolidation, and the limited solute misfit reduces the propensity for crack‑initiating stress concentrations. Residual porosity is modest, and any Cr‑rich secondary phases appear as thin, discontinuous films that do not severely impede dislocation glide, thereby supporting higher elongation. Conversely, the Hf‑Re‑containing composition introduces markedly larger atomic size mismatches and higher electron‑density contrast, intensifying solid‑solution strengthening but also generating pronounced lattice strain fields. Spark‑plasma sintering of HfReVTiCr tends to produce a bimodal grain distribution with coarse, recrystallized grains interspersed with fine, Hf‑rich precipitates that act as potent barriers to slip and promote early void nucleation at grain‑boundary triple points. The combined effect of elevated lattice distortion, increased precipitate volume fraction, and occasional intergranular cracking leads to a plausible trend of lower ductility for HfReVTiCr relative to WTaVCr.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: elongation at fracture and the microstructural features that promote or limit ductility

text: During the directed energy deposition of the refractory high entropy alloy MoHfVReCrTaNb, a series of build passes were executed at a laser power of 400 W and a scan speed of 600 mm s⁻¹, producing fully dense parts with minimal porosity. Post‑solidification, the microstructure exhibited a predominantly BCC matrix with fine equiaxed grains (~3 µm) interspersed by nanoscale precipitates rich in Cr–Ta and Hf–Re. Compression tests on polished cross‑sections revealed a yield stress significantly higher than the corresponding tensile yield stress, with an asymmetry factor exceeding 1.4, indicative of a pronounced hardening under compression. Nanoindentation mapping across the surface captured a heterogeneous hardness distribution; regions coincident with the Cr–Ta rich precipitates showed elevated hardness values (~1.2 GPa) and modulus (~260 GPa), whereas the BCC matrix displayed lower values (~0.9 GPa hardness, 240 GPa modulus). The correlation between local hardness maxima and compositional segregation suggests that solid‑solution strengthening and precipitate‑induced lattice distortion reinforce compressive resistance, while tensile failure is facilitated by the softer matrix regions, accounting for the observed asymmetry.
processing_route: laser additive manufacturing (directed energy deposition)
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy ReVHfTiTaW was synthesized by high‑energy mechanical alloying of elemental powders and subsequently consolidated through hot‑pressing at temperatures sufficient to promote densification while limiting grain coarsening. Microstructural examination reveals a predominantly single‑phase BCC matrix with a narrow grain size distribution that can be tuned from the sub‑micron to several microns by adjusting the hot‑press dwell time. Systematic hardness and uniaxial tensile testing demonstrate that finer grains systematically enhance both hardness and yield strength, consistent with a Hall‑Petch relationship in which grain‑boundary barriers impede dislocation motion more effectively as the average grain diameter decreases. The observed trend is amplified by the intrinsic lattice distortion arising from the multi‑principal elements, which raises the critical resolved shear stress and synergistically interacts with grain‑boundary strengthening. Consequently, the alloy exhibits a pronounced trade‑off: reductions in grain size yield substantial gains in strength and hardness, while modest grain growth leads to a measurable softening, highlighting grain‑size engineering as a key lever for tailoring mechanical performance in ReVHfTiTaW.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing

text: The vacuum‑induction‑melted TaWMoCrV alloy exhibits a markedly higher Young’s modulus than the simpler TaZrV system, a consequence of its more extensive transition‑metal network and the associated increase in directional d‑electron bonding. Incorporating tungsten and molybdenum introduces additional high‑valence, stiff BCC sublattices that raise the average valence electron concentration, strengthening metallic covalency and reducing lattice compliance. Chromium and vanadium further contribute to solid‑solution hardening and enhance the overall bond density, while the presence of tantalum provides a heavy, incompressible backbone. In contrast, TaZrV relies on a ternary mixture where zirconium, a larger, more ductile Hf‑group element, introduces greater lattice distortion and a higher proportion of metallic‑ionic character, which softens the elastic response. Consequently, the TaWMoCrV composition is expected to trend toward a larger Young’s modulus owing to its richer d‑band overlap and reduced bond polarity, whereas TaZrV, with its lighter, more pliable sublattice, should display a comparatively lower modulus.
processing_route: vacuum induction melting

text: The TiZrWTaVCr alloy, produced by repeated arc‑melting and rapid solidification through drop casting, adopts a body‑centered cubic matrix that remains largely single‑phase but exhibits pronounced lattice distortion from the five constituent refractory elements. The high degree of atomic size mismatch generates a stiff, yet brittle, BCC framework in which crack initiation is strongly governed by the local stress concentration at notches; consequently, the material displays marked notch sensitivity, with even shallow notches precipitating rapid fracture propagation. Grain refinement achieved during drop casting mitigates this effect by increasing the number of grain boundaries that can impede crack advance, modestly elevating the apparent fracture toughness relative to coarse‑grained counterparts. However, the absence of ductile secondary phases and the persistence of residual porosity limit the capacity of these boundaries to blunt cracks, so the fracture toughness remains low and highly dependent on notch geometry, underscoring the critical role of microstructural control in reducing notch‑driven brittleness in this refractory high‑entropy system.
processing_route: arc melting followed by drop casting
subtopic: notch sensitivity and its relation to fracture toughness in brittle BCC compositions

text: The suction‑cast billets of HfZrNbV and CrReTaTi were produced in a sealed copper mold under high‑purity argon, the melt being poured at 2000 °C and solidified within seconds; subsequent polishing removed the surface oxide layer before indentation and tensile testing. Microstructural inspection revealed that HfZrNbV retained a relatively coarse, equiaxed BCC matrix with modest lattice distortion, whereas CrReTaTi displayed a finer grain structure and pronounced solid‑solution hardening due to the larger atomic size mismatch among Cr, Re, Ta, and Ti. According to Tabor’s correlation, the alloy exhibiting higher indentation hardness also manifests a higher 0.2 % yield stress because the same resistance to dislocation glide governs both phenomena. Consequently, the CrReTaTi specimen, with its greater grain‑boundary area and stronger distortion‑based barrier to slip, is expected to plot above HfZrNbV on a hardness‑yield strength diagram, while the latter’s comparatively lower hardness reflects its lower yield strength despite similar processing conditions.

subtopic: the qualitative correlation between hardness and yield strength (Tabor-type reasoning)

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy ReHfW, produced by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot‑pressing, exhibits a distinctive oxidation response that is governed by its complex solid‑solution matrix and the intrinsic affinity of its constituent elements for oxygen. The dense, near‑single‑phase BCC structure generated during hot pressing limits diffusion pathways, yet the substantial lattice distortion introduced by the size mismatch between Re, Hf and W creates a high density of defect sites that act as preferential nucleation points for oxide formation. Early-stage oxidation is dominated by the rapid formation of a thin, adherent Re‑rich sub‑oxide layer, which serves as a barrier to further ingress of oxygen. Beneath this, the more sluggish Hf and W oxides develop as a porous, multi‑layered scale that thickens with exposure time. Grain refinement achieved during milling enhances the continuity of the protective Re‑oxide, while residual porosity at grain boundaries can accelerate localized spallation of the outer scale, exposing fresh metal and accelerating degradation. Overall, the balance between a coherent Re‑oxide surface film and the underlying mixed Hf‑W oxide assemblage dictates the alloy’s high‑temperature oxidation resistance.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: oxidation behavior at elevated temperature

text: The MoNbTiWVRe refractory high‑entropy alloy was synthesized in a quartz‑sealed, argon‑backfilled chamber using vacuum induction melting to avoid oxidation of the constituent elements. After three melt‑stirring cycles the melt was drop‑cast into a copper mould and subsequently homogenized at temperatures just below the solidus to promote diffusion without triggering extensive grain growth. Metallographic examination revealed a primary body‑centered cubic matrix whose hardness varied systematically with the volume fraction of a W‑rich intermetallic lamellae that formed on cooling. Specimens containing a higher proportion of the secondary phase exhibited a noticeably tougher response to indentation, indicating that the dispersed hard lamellae impede dislocation motion more effectively than the solid‑solution‑strengthened matrix alone. In contrast, alloys in which the intermetallics were sparsely distributed or partially dissolved during the homogenization step displayed a comparatively lower hardness, reflecting the dominant role of lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening when secondary phases are minimized.

text: Vacuum induction melting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy NbHfMoZr followed by hot extrusion yields a single‑phase body‑centered cubic microstructure with uniformly distributed lattice distortion. The measured Young’s modulus increases progressively with the relative molar fraction of the hard, high‑valence‑electron‑count elements Hf and Mo, while the softer Nb component exerts a diluting effect on the modulus through its lower electron density. First‑principles calculations indicate that the Nb–Hf and Mo–Zr bonds contribute the most to the overall shear stiffness due to their short, highly covalent character, whereas the Nb–Zr interactions are comparatively weaker and reduce the elastic response. The observed modulus trend is thus governed by the interplay between the electron‑count‑driven bonding strength and the compositional tuning of the lattice distortion, which modulates the electron density and the effective atomic packing factor. These results suggest that fine‑tuning the Nb:Hf:Mo:Zr ratio offers a viable pathway to tailor the elastic properties of NbHfMoZr for high‑temperature structural applications.

text: The suction‑cast TiNbReZr alloy exhibits a markedly higher compressive yield response than the CrZrRe counterpart, a difference that can be traced to the combined effects of lattice distortion and solid‑solution strengthening. Ti, Nb and Zr contribute comparable atomic radii, producing a moderately distorted body‑centered cubic matrix that is further stiffened by the addition of Re, whose large atomic size and high melting point generate substantial resistance to dislocation motion under compression. In CrZrRe, the presence of Cr introduces a stronger tendency toward BCC ordering and a modestly lower overall distortion; the resulting matrix is more prone to early activation of slip systems, leading to a reduced compressive yield stress. Moreover, TiNbReZr typically retains a finer dendritic cell size after rapid solidification, which raises the barrier for dislocation nucleation in compression, whereas CrZrRe often shows coarser segregation bands that facilitate slip. This microstructural asymmetry also explains the commonly observed tensile‑compressive yield offset: TiNbReZr’s enhanced compression strength is accompanied by a relatively lower tensile yield, reflecting the anisotropic constraint of the suction‑cast microstructure, while CrZrRe displays a more symmetric but overall softer response in both loading modes.
processing_route: suction casting under an inert argon atmosphere
subtopic: compressive yield behavior, including asymmetry between tensile and compressive yield response

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy HfVZrWMoCrRe, produced by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot pressing, exhibits a thermodynamic landscape that favors single‑phase formation despite its complex chemistry. Calculations of the mixing enthalpy reveal a modestly negative value, indicating that the constituent elements engage in favorable binary interactions without driving extensive compound segregation; the broad distribution of atomic sizes and the comparable electronegativities of Hf, V, Zr, W, Mo, Cr, and Re further reduce the propensity for intermetallic precipitation. Simultaneously, the valence electron concentration (VEC) resides in a range that stabilizes a body‑centered cubic lattice, balancing the d‑electron contributions from the transition metals and the s‑p hybridization of Hf and Zr. This VEC regime suppresses the formation of ordered B2 or Laves phases, allowing the configurational entropy to dominate the Gibbs free energy and promote a chemically homogeneous solid solution. The synergy of a slightly exothermic mixing enthalpy and an optimal VEC thus underpins the observed microstructural uniformity in the hot‑pressed HfVZrWMoCrRe alloy.
processing_route: mechanical alloying followed by hot pressing
subtopic: thermodynamic considerations (mixing enthalpy, valence electron concentration)

text: The powder‑metallurgy route followed by spark‑plasma sintering produced a dense ReHfZrTiTaCr alloy in which the primary body‑centred cubic lattice is interrupted by nanoscale Re‑rich precipitates distributed coherently within the matrix. Microhardness measurements reveal a pronounced increase relative to the single‑phase baseline, and this hardening correlates with the volume fraction of the Re‑rich phase: finer, more uniformly spaced precipitates yield a higher hardness, whereas coarsening or agglomeration leads to a slight decline. Tensile testing with extensometer monitoring shows that samples with the highest precipitate density maintain substantial elongation before fracture, suggesting that the coherent precipitates impede dislocation motion without introducing significant brittleness. When the precipitate size grows beyond the critical spacing for coherent strengthening, the alloy exhibits reduced plastic strain and a more pronounced brittle response, highlighting the delicate balance between hardening and ductility governed by secondary phase morphology.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering
subtopic: the effect of secondary phase or precipitate content on hardness

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy MoTaRe, when consolidated by powder metallurgy and spark‑plasma‑sintered to near‑theoretical density, exhibits a tensile response that is strongly governed by temperature‑driven changes in its lattice‑distortion and dislocation‑mobility mechanisms. In ASTM E8‑type pull‑out tests, the alloy retains a relatively high yield strength at ambient temperature because the severe atomic size mismatch among Mo, Ta and Re produces a pronounced solid‑solution hardening field, while the fine, equiaxed grains generated during rapid sintering further impede dislocation glide. As the test temperature is raised into the intermediate range, thermally activated cross‑slip and climb become increasingly facile; the yield point therefore begins to drop, yet the alloy still outperforms conventional refractory steels because the retained high‑temperature lattice friction and the modest amount of Re‑rich precipitates continue to block dislocation motion. Approaching the upper part of the service window, the tensile strength decays more rapidly as recovery and dynamic recrystallization soften the microstructure, although the intrinsic high melting points of the constituent elements delay the onset of catastrophic softening, preserving useful load‑bearing capacity up to temperatures where diffusion‑controlled mechanisms dominate.
processing_route: powder metallurgy and spark plasma sintering

text: TaMoHfRe belongs to the class of refractory high‑entropy alloys in which the configurational entropy of mixing is comparable to, or exceeds, the enthalpic penalties associated with forming a solid solution.  During mechanical alloying the elemental powders are repeatedly fractured and welded, allowing the five‑component system to approach a homogeneous distribution before hot‑press consolidation eliminates residual porosity.  Thermodynamically, the overall mixing enthalpy of Ta–Mo–Hf–Re is modestly negative because the binary interactions among the transition metals are largely metallic and lack strong compound‑forming tendencies; this promotes single‑phase BCC retention during the high‑temperature press.  Simultaneously, the valence‑electron‑concentration (VEC) of the alloy falls within the range that stabilizes a body‑centered cubic lattice, ensuring that electronic band filling does not drive a transformation to more complex ordered structures.  The combination of high configurational entropy, low‑magnitude mixing enthalpy, and a VEC that favors BCC symmetry therefore rationalizes why TaMoHfRe can be densified into a chemically disordered, refractory matrix with minimal phase segregation.

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy WTaMoNbZrVTi was carried out in a glove‑box filled with high‑purity argon (p < 10⁻⁶ mbar). The master ingot was melted in an induction furnace to 2500 °C, then transferred through a tungsten nozzle into a pre‑heated copper mold, allowing rapid solidification at cooling rates of ~10⁶ K s⁻¹. Resulting micrographs revealed a near‑body‑centred‑cubic solid solution with nanoscale W‑rich lamellae and trace Mo‑rich precipitates. Mechanical testing of compression samples indicated a yield strength exceeding 3.5 GPa, while Vickers microhardness measurements gave values above 4.5 GPa. According to Tabor’s relation, the high hardness is consistent with the elevated yield strength, suggesting that the fine lamellar architecture and lattice distortion imposed by the five principal elements jointly provide solid‑solution and precipitation strengthening, while the minimal porosity achieved by the inert atmosphere preserves load‑carrying capacity.

text: Suction casting of the refractory high‑entropy alloy TaNbZrTiVMoRe under an inert argon atmosphere produced a fully dense, coarse‑grained BCC microstructure with minimal porosity. Resonant ultrasound spectroscopy revealed a high elastic modulus that increased with grain refinement, consistent with the large lattice parameters of Ta and Re and the pronounced solid‑solution strengthening from the high configurational entropy. Notch‑toughness measurements on compact tension specimens showed a pronounced reduction in fracture toughness compared to unnotched samples, highlighting the alloy’s intrinsic notch sensitivity. Microstructural analysis indicated that fracture initiation occurred preferentially at grain boundary junctions where local stress concentration was amplified, and that the brittle BCC matrix lacked ductile secondary phases to blunt cracks. The combination of a high elastic modulus, limited plasticity, and a fine but untextured grain structure therefore drives a sharp drop in toughness under notched conditions, underscoring the need for grain‑size control or the introduction of minor ductile reinforcements to mitigate notch sensitivity in TaNbZrTiVMoRe.

text: Laser additive manufacturing by directed energy deposition was employed to fabricate two refractory high‑entropy alloy (HEA) feedstocks, VTiHfReTaZr and HfTaWZrMoNbV, enabling direct comparison of strain‑rate‑dependent strength behavior. Both systems exhibit dense, fine equiaxed microstructures with a pronounced solid‑solution matrix and minimal porosity, yet their constituent atomic size mismatches and valence electron concentrations differ markedly. The VTiHfReTaZr alloy, containing the light V and the larger Hf, tends toward a lower average lattice distortion, resulting in a more compliant lattice that can accommodate dislocation glide more readily at elevated strain rates; consequently, its flow stress increases moderately with strain rate, indicating a weaker strain‑rate sensitivity. In contrast, the HfTaWZrMoNbV composition harbors a higher degree of size mismatch and a higher valence electron concentration, leading to stronger lattice friction and more pronounced dislocation pile‑up under dynamic loading. Therefore, HfTaWZrMoNbV is expected to display a steeper rise in strength with increasing strain rate, reflecting its higher intrinsic strain‑rate sensitivity relative to VTiHfReTaZr.

text: The refractory alloy MoTiHfWTaCrNb, when produced by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated by hot pressing, typically exhibits a fine, equiaxed grain structure that evolves as a function of the pressing temperature and hold time. Because the constituent elements differ markedly in atomic radius, the resulting solid‑solution matrix is heavily distorted, so each grain boundary acts as an effective barrier to dislocation motion; consequently, decreasing the average grain diameter raises both the flow stress and the indentation resistance in a manner consistent with a Hall‑Petch relationship. In practice, rapid consolidation at lower temperatures preserves the nanocrystalline substructure generated during milling, yielding higher hardness and yield strength, whereas prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures promotes grain growth, reducing the density of obstacles and softening the alloy. The presence of minor secondary phases at grain edges can further impede slip, but the dominant trend remains that finer grains enhance strength and hardness, while coarser grains diminish them.

text: The refractory high‑entropy alloy ZrCrRe, when produced by high‑energy mechanical alloying and consolidated through hot pressing, develops a heavily distorted BCC lattice that confers excellent intrinsic oxidation resistance, yet its surface still demands a protective strategy for sustained service above 1000 °C. Because the alloy’s constituent elements differ markedly in affinity for oxygen, a thin, adherent oxide scale composed of Cr₂O₃ and ZrO₂ tends to form spontaneously; however, the scale’s adherence can be compromised by thermal cycling and residual porosity left from powder consolidation. To reinforce this barrier, researchers commonly apply a secondary ceramic coating such as TiAlN or Al₂O₃ by physical vapor deposition, which supplies a dense, diffusion‑slow layer that accommodates the underlying lattice expansion through graded compositional interfaces. The high lattice distortion in ZrCrRe promotes a fine grain structure that enhances the bonding between the coating and substrate, while residual compressive stresses generated during hot pressing help to close micro‑cracks, further improving the coating’s resistance to spallation during prolonged high‑temperature exposure.

text: Both MoTaZrVTiRe and TiHfWZrNb are equiatomic refractory high‑entropy alloys that inherit a body‑centered‑cubic matrix from the dominant transition‑metal constituents, yet their work‑hardening responses diverge because of contrasting lattice‑distortion fields and precipitate populations generated during arc‑melting and rapid solidification. The Mo‑rich system contains a larger atomic‑size mismatch (Mo, Ta, V, Ti, Re, Zr) and therefore experiences stronger solid‑solution strengthening; the resulting high dislocation friction stress promotes a steep early‑stage hardening slope, but the limited solubility of Re and Zr often yields fine, dispersed intermetallic particles that act as strong barriers to dislocation motion, sustaining the hardening rate to larger strains. In contrast, TiHfWZrNb exhibits a comparatively lower size mismatch and a higher propensity for the formation of coarse, blocky Hf‑rich precipitates; these act as effective pinning sites at low strain but become bypassed more readily, yielding a gentler work‑hardening curve. Consequently, the MoTaZrVTiRe alloy is expected to display a higher overall work‑hardening capacity, while TiHfWZrNb should harden more modestly throughout tensile loading.
